sens: One who lacks material resources, money, or possessions
Who is weak, fragile, without physical or moral strength
Who is of little importance, thin or lean
Who is lowered, oppressed, defenseless before the powerful
H1800.detail: 1. The poor is one who has no wealth, who lacks the necessities. It is a material condition: without money, land, or means of subsistence (Proverbs 10:15: "The ruin of the poor is his poverty"). 2. Weak means without strength, without physical or moral vigor. The house of Saul "was weakening" while David was strengthening (2 Samuel 3:1), or a body becomes thin and exhausted. 3. The image can be that of something small, thin, or insubstantial: a light rain, a meager harvest, a small fortune. 4. Figuratively, the poor is one who is lowered, defenseless, crushed by the powerful and the wicked. It is one who cries out to God because he has no one to help him (Job 34:28: "They have made the cry of the poor rise to God").
H1800.origine: The root דַּל reveals the primary image of something low, lowered, hence the idea of weakness and poverty. The word is related to the idea of "descending" or "being little." In biblical Hebrew, this word primarily expresses the state of one who is without resources and protection, a natural object of God's compassion and a duty of justice for others.
H1800.emploi: The word appears 46 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Proverbs, Psalms, and the prophets. In the code of the Law (Exodus, Leviticus), it designates the poor who has the right to equal justice (Exodus 23:3; Leviticus 19:15), without discrimination. In Proverbs, it illustrates either the misfortune of poverty (Proverbs 10:15) or the moral duty to have pity (Proverbs 14:31: "Oppressing the poor is insulting to his Maker"). The prophets denounce the oppression of the poor as a serious sin (Isaiah 10:2; Amos 2:7, 4:1). The Messiah is to defend the poor with equity (Isaiah 11:4).
H1800.portee: This word reminds believers that God has a special love for those who suffer and are defenseless. The condition of the poor tests the justice and mercy of each person: to despise or oppress him is to offend God Himself who created him (Proverbs 14:31). Jesus and his disciples will embody this preferential love for the poor, those who need salvation and compassion.

sens: To leap with a quick movement of the body
To overcome an obstacle by jumping
To leap over, to quickly surpass
To rush with eagerness
H1801.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the physical movement of jumping: leaping from one place to another by propelling oneself with the legs. In Song of Solomon 2:8, the beloved "jumps" on the mountains as one would describe an animal leaping with agility.
2. To overcome an obstacle by jumping over it means to jump in the sense of crossing in a leap: the psalmist says "to leap over a wall" (Psalms 18:30), not by demolishing it, but by surpassing it in a leap, an image of the invincibility that God provides.
3. To leap over means to pass over something without stopping, often in an impetuous or malicious manner. In Zephaniah 1:9, "jumping over the threshold" describes a sacrilegious violation of the dwelling, a crossing of boundaries with contempt.
4. The figurative nuance of eagerness and haste appears when one "rushes" with impetuosity: the movement of jumping expresses vehemence, the speed of action.
H1801.origine: The Hebrew root dalag evokes the sudden and vigorous movement of a leap. It belongs to the family of verbs of quick movement. The basic image is that of jumping or leaping: a gesture that quickly crosses a distance, either physically or figuratively. The Hebrew language often uses this verb to describe animals that jump (deer, gazelles) or to evoke rapid and energetic movements.
H1801.emploi: The verb jump appears 5 times in the Bible. It first describes physical and real jumps: the beloved who leaps on the mountains (Song of Solomon 2:8), the lame man healed who "will leap like a deer" (Isaiah 35:6, a prophecy of restoration). It is also used figuratively to mean surpassing or overcoming: the psalmist who "leaps over a wall" with God (Psalms 18:30 and its parallel in 2 Samuel 22:30). The verb can also describe an act of impious surpassing: in Zephaniah 1:9, "jumping over the threshold" is an act of transgression and profanation. In each context, the word carries the idea of a quick movement that crosses or surpasses.
H1801.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that God gives His people the strength to overcome obstacles, just as one jumps over a wall. It also evokes the promised restoration: the weak body will be capable of leaps of joy. But it also warns that crossing the boundaries that God has set is a grave act of rebellion. It is a word of action and energy that speaks to the heart.

sens: To draw water from a well or a spring
To obtain, extract something from a reserve
To draw from one's inner resources, to explore one's thoughts
H1802.detail:
1. The primary and concrete meaning: to draw is to take water from a well or a fountain to drink or use. The daughters of the priest of Midian came to "draw" water every day (Exodus 2:16); Moses himself helped them to "draw" water to water their father's flock (Exodus 2:19). It is the image of a hand going down into the well and coming up with the precious liquid.
2. By extension, to draw means to extract or obtain something from a source, a reserve. The concrete gesture of the well becomes an image for everything one draws from a depth.
3. Figuratively, to draw refers to the act of exploring, searching within one's thoughts or heart: "The wise man knows how to draw" from the deep designs of the human heart (Proverbs 20:5). It is to dig within oneself to extract wisdom, understanding, hidden intentions.
H1802.origine: The Hebrew verb דָּלָה (dalah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of descending and pulling up — the movement of the arm that plunges the bucket into the well and brings it back filled. This image of "drawing" remains the primary use of the word in the Bible. The root belongs to a group of verbs that speak of movement from bottom to top, of what comes out from a depth.
H1802.emploi: The verb dalah appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the concrete or figurative sense of "drawing." Three uses are concrete and narrative: in the two passages from Exodus 2, where it is about drawing water from the well for the flocks. The use in Proverbs 20:5 shifts to the figurative: drawing from the designs of the heart means probing its depth as one would draw from a well. The word thus remains attached to this image of the hand that goes down and comes up, of the visible drawing from the hidden.
H1802.portee: Drawing reminds us that wisdom, like living water, is found in the depths — one must seek, question, and not remain on the surface. For the Christian, it is an invitation to dig into one's own spiritual life, to explore the thoughts of God revealed in His Word, and to extract the water that refreshes. The humble and patient gesture of drawing also speaks of dependence: we draw our strength and wisdom from a source that surpasses us.

sens: A filament of keratinous material that grows on the head and body of humans and animals
The collection of hair covering the head
A thread or strand in the weaving
H1803A.detail:
1. Hair is the fine and slender filament that naturally grows on the skin, particularly on the head. In the Song of Solomon, the beauty of the beloved's hair is compared to purple, a royal color: it is a charming and precious detail of beauty (Song of Solomon 7:6).
2. Hair refers to the entirety of the hair, a symbol of seduction and vitality. When the psalmist says that the king is "entangled by the curls" of hair, he shows how beauty captivates and attracts (Song of Solomon 7:6).
3. The word can also refer to the threads of the weft in a fabric: the horizontal threads that are passed through the vertical threads (the warp) on a loom. Isaiah uses this image to express that his life is "cut off" like a weaver cuts his finished work, a sign of imminent death (Isaiah 38:12).
H1803A.origine: The Hebrew word dalah literally means "thread" or "filament," hence its dual usage: hair on one hand (keratin threads), the weft of a fabric on the other (threads of wool or linen). The common image is of something fine, long, and slender. This root is related to words expressing weakness or suspension, as a thread hangs and can easily break.
H1803A.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Song of Solomon 7:6, it refers to the beloved's hair, a poetic detail of her beauty. In Isaiah 38:12, Hezekiah, mortally ill, uses the same word in the technical sense of weaving to describe his life as a fabric that the weaver will cut: it is a striking allegory of approaching death. The same word thus navigates from poetic concrete (hair) to metaphorical technical (the weft).
H1803A.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible views human beauty without guilt (the beloved's hair is admired), but also that our life is fragile and limited like a thread that can be cut at any moment. For the Christian, it is an invitation not to place trust in the beauty or duration of this world, but in the hand of God who holds all our days.

sens: Devoid of wealth, without material means
Thin, emaciated, of weak appearance
The resource-less people left after a captivity or judgment
H1803B.detail:
1. This word primarily designates someone who lacks money, goods, or material security. It is the state of one who has nothing or almost nothing. For example, after the captivity of Jerusalem, the king of Babylon "left as vine dressers and farmers some of the poorest of the land" (2 Kings 25:12), meaning those too weak or landless to be useful as slaves.
2. The word also applies to what is thin, sickly, without strength. Pharaoh sees "seven other cows that came up after them, ugly and gaunt, and thin" (Genesis 41:19) — these cows are poor in the sense that they are thin and weakened.
3. Collectively, the word designates the common people, those who remain after the strong, the rich, and the craftsmen have been taken away. During the deportation to Babylon, "only the poor people of the land were left" (2 Kings 24:14), meaning those deemed too insignificant to be deported.
H1803B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of being weak, sickly, defenseless. The feminine form with the suffix -ah gives the adjective or noun "poor." It is a common word to express the material and social condition of the common people in Israel.
H1803B.emploi: This word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the accounts of captivity (2 Kings 24-25 and Jeremiah 40, 52). In Genesis 41:19, it describes the thin cows in Pharaoh's dream. In all other usages, it designates the poor people who remain in Judah after the Babylonians have taken away the leaders, warriors, and craftsmen — it is the common people left behind, defenseless and without resources. The context shows that the poor are those judged too weak to be of any utility as captives or slaves.
H1803B.portee: This word invites the reader to see as God sees: not with disdain, but with attention. The poor are often at the heart of divine concern. Here, we see that even after the judgment of captivity, God does not abandon them — Jeremiah is sent to them, and leaders are established to govern them. This reminds believers that the small, the weak, the forgotten are never invisible in the eyes of God.

sens: Stir the water, make it murky and agitated
Agitate, make swirl by pouring or stirring
Figuratively: disturb, disrupt a state of calm or rest
H1804.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to stir the water to make it murky. In Ezekiel 32:2, Pharaoh is compared to a crocodile that plunges into the rivers and stirs the waters with its feet — the image evokes water losing its clarity and becoming muddy through movement.
2. The verb designates the concrete action of agitating, making swirl: this is what happens when one stirs the water or when an animal splashes in it. It is the water itself that becomes agitated and murky, not just soiled.
3. Figuratively, to trouble means to disturb the calm or established order. In Ezekiel 32:13, after Pharaoh's death, no one will trouble the waters anymore — meaning that peace will return, and agitation and domination will cease.
H1804.origine: The Hebrew verb דָּלַח (dalach) comes from a root that describes the movement of stirring or agitating. Its basic image is that of water being troubled by plunging feet or stirring. The family of the word carries this idea of physical agitation and loss of clarity.
H1804.emploi: The verb appears twice in the book of Ezekiel, both in Ezekiel 32, in a prophetic lament against the Pharaoh of Egypt. In the first usage (Ezekiel 32:2), it describes the actions of the living Pharaoh — he troubles the waters of the rivers with his feet, like a powerful crocodile that dominates and stirs everything. In the second usage (Ezekiel 32:13), the same verb is used in the future tense to say that after his fall, no human or animal foot will trouble the waters anymore — which signifies the end of his tyrannical reign and the return of calm. The nuance between the two passages is this: first a dominating and destructive action, then its definitive cessation.
H1804.portee: This word reveals how the Bible uses the image of troubled water to speak of disorder, oppressive domination, and the disturbance of peace. It teaches us that God's judgment on tyrants brings rest — when the one who troubles ceases, the waters regain calm. For the believer, this is an encouragement: the Lord puts an end to the powers that agitate and trouble the world.

sens: Container used to draw or transport water
Image of great abundance of water
Symbol of smallness or insignificance
H1805.detail:
1. The bucket is a simple container, often made of wood or metal, used to draw water from a well or spring and transport it. In Numbers 24:7, buckets represent the reservoirs that hold and pour out the abundant water of a fertile land: the image evokes a wealth of life and prosperity.
2. By extension, the word "bucket" represents the capacity to hold a large quantity of water, hence its use to express abundance and fertility. The overflowing waters from the buckets symbolize a generous blessing.
3. In contrast, in Isaiah 40:15, a single drop from a bucket becomes the image of extreme smallness: the nations, as powerful as they may seem, are but insignificant drops in the eyes of God. This poetic reversal shows how the same ordinary object can measure both abundance and insignificance depending on perspective.
H1805.origine: The Hebrew word דְּלִי (deli) is linked to the domestic and pastoral world of the ancient Near East. Its etymology refers to the idea of drawing, pulling towards oneself (from a root meaning "to suspend" or "to hang"), which corresponds well to the function of the bucket that is lowered into the well with the help of a rope. It is a concrete word, designating the everyday object found in any community with access to water.
H1805.emploi: The word דְּלִי appears only twice in the Old Testament, in the two provided passages. In Numbers 24:7, it is in the prophecy of Balaam about Israel, where the overflowing water from the buckets represents the divine prosperity granted to the people; here, the bucket is an element of wealth and blessing. In Isaiah 40:15, the same bucket changes function: a drop of water remains a drop, even taken from the largest bucket in the world, to signify the insignificance of human powers in the face of God's infinite greatness. These two uses show how a simple object becomes a vector of two opposing spiritual messages: blessed abundance on one side, forced humility on the other.
H1805.portee: These two passages invite the reader to perceive their condition in two lights. With Balaam, they discover that God's blessing fills generously like overflowing buckets: it is concrete, tangible, abundant. With Isaiah, they learn to relativize the importance of earthly powers and human realities, however impressive they may be, for in the eyes of the Creator, they weigh like a drop of water. This contrast reminds us that trusting in God means moving from visible and limited wealth to a true perspective on what really matters.

sens: A man from the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy, son of Eljoenaï
H1806G.detail: Delaja is a descendant of the Davidic royalty, listed among the seven sons of Eljoenaï in the genealogy of the kings of Judah (1 Chronicles 3:24). He lived at a time when the kingdom was divided between the Northern Kingdom (Israel) and the Southern Kingdom (Judah), in the period following Solomon.
H1806G.origine: The name Delaja means "Jehovah has drawn" or "Jehovah has delivered": it combines the divine name Jah (Jehovah) with the verb that evokes the action of drawing or delivering. It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that carries the name of God, a common reflex in Jewish onomastics.
H1806G.emploi: Delaja is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:24, in the detailed genealogy of the descendants of King David. He is presented as one of the seven sons of Eljoenaï, himself a descendant of Shaltiel and thus linked to the weakened royal lineage that survived after the exile. This passage indicates his historical existence and his place in the royal genealogy of Judah, without providing further details about his life or actions.

sens: Priest during the time of David, leader of the twenty-third group of service in the temple
H1806H.detail: 1. Delaja is a Levitical priest living under the reign of King David. He is the leader of the twenty-third group among the twenty-four divisions of priests established for temple service. In 1 Chronicles 24:18, it reads: "the twenty-third, to Delaja; the twenty-fourth, to Maaziah." These divisions ensured that various services of worship in Jerusalem were carried out in turn throughout the year.
H1806H.origine: The name Delaja means "Jehovah has drawn" or "Jehovah has liberated," composed of the Hebrew Dal (to draw, to deliver) and Yah (abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah). It expresses God's saving action towards the named person.
H1806H.emploi: Delaja appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 24:18. He is listed among the twenty-four leaders of the priestly divisions that David established to organize the ongoing service of the temple. This list shows how the king sought to precisely structure religious functions and maintain order in the house of God.

sens: Leader of a family of exiles
Family returning from Babylonian captivity
H1806I.detail:
1. Delaja is a family leader among the exiles from Babylon who sought to be recognized as Israelites upon their return under Zerubbabel. In the census lists, his family counts between 642 and 652 members (according to the two records in Ezra and Nehemiah), making it a significant community among those claiming to belong to Israel without being able to prove their genealogy (Ezra 2:60).
2. The name Delaja appears twice in the official documents of the return from exile — once in the register of Ezra and once in that of Nehemiah — which list the families returned from captivity and claiming the right to participate in the reconstruction of the temple and the Israelite nation (Nehemiah 7:62).
H1806I.origine: The name Delaja means "Yahweh has drawn" or "Yahweh has lifted," formed from two Hebrew elements: "Yah" (the name of God) and "laya" (to draw, to lift). It is a typical theophoric name, meaning it proclaims an action of God. This type of name was common in Israel to express trust in divine intervention or recognition of deliverance.
H1806I.emploi: Delaja is mentioned exclusively in the lists of the return from Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:60 and Nehemiah 7:62). It designates the leader of a family that had requested to be registered among the Israelites returned from captivity, but whose ancestry could not be established with certainty — a particular and somewhat ambiguous status within the reconstructing community. The two parallel passages provide slightly different numbers for this family, likely reflecting counts made at different times during the gradual return of the exiles.

sens: Man from the time of exile and the return to Jerusalem
H1806J.detail: Delaja is a minor character mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when Nehemiah is rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem after the exile. He is the father of Schemaiah and the son of Mehetabel. Schemaiah, his son, attempts to persuade Nehemiah to enter the temple for safety, claiming that assassins are seeking him (Nehemiah 6:10). This scheme to compromise Nehemiah shows that Delaja was the father of a man who held a position of influence in Jerusalem during the return from Babylonian exile.
H1806J.origine: The name Delaja literally means "Jehovah has drawn" or "Jehovah has raised," composed of the Hebrew root meaning "to draw, to lift" and the divine name Yah. This name expresses the confidence that God raises and delivers His people, particularly resonant for a family living at the time of the return from exile.
H1806J.emploi: Delaja appears only once in the biblical text, in Nehemiah 6:10. He is presented as the father of Schemaiah, a character who attempted to dissuade Nehemiah from continuing his reconstruction project. Schemaiah claimed to act on behalf of his father and influential figures, but Nehemiah exposed this attempt at manipulation as a ruse to compromise him. Delaja thus represents one of the influential families among those who returned from exile, but who did not wholeheartedly support Nehemiah's work.

sens: Jewish figure from the time of Jeremiah
Son of Schemaeja, officer in the court of Jehoiakim
Man who interceded to preserve the scroll of Jeremiah
H1806K.detail:
1. Delaja is a historical figure attested in Judea at the time when the kingdom was divided, specifically during the time of the prophet Jeremiah and King Jehoiakim.
2. He is the son of Schemaeja, a man of high rank in the Jewish hierarchy, which explains his presence among the leaders gathered in the royal court (Jeremiah 36:12).
3. He is known for having, along with Elnathan and Guemaria, attempted to prevent the king from burning the scroll containing the words of Jeremiah, thus showing a certain goodwill towards the prophetic word, even though he was not heard by the king (Jeremiah 36:25).
H1806K.origine: The name means "Jehovah has drawn" or "Jehovah has attracted," composed of the divine element Yah (abbreviation of the divine name) and the verb dalah which expresses the action of drawing or pulling (notably water from a well). This name expresses the trust that the parent placed in God, thanking Him for His protective or salvific action at the birth or at the time of the name's choice.
H1806K.emploi: Delaja appears twice in the book of Jeremiah, in verses 12 and 25 of chapter 36, both concerning the same event: the presentation of the prophetic scroll in the court of King Jehoiakim. He is first mentioned as one of the leaders sitting in the secretary's chamber when Micaiah reads the scroll. Then, he is named among those who interceded with the king to ask him not to burn the book, a courageous step since the king opposed this plea and rejected this request.
H1806K.portee: The story of Delaja illustrates how, even in the realms of political power, some men can recognize the value and importance of the word of God, despite the resistance of the sovereign. His intercession, although unsuccessful, testifies that prophecy was not without a voice in the royal court, and that God raised up men to defend His word, regardless of the immediate results.

sens: Philistine woman, mistress and wife of Samson
She who discovered the secret of Samson's superhuman strength
She who betrayed Samson to the Philistines
H1807.detail:
1. Delila is a woman living in the time of the judges in Israel, in the valley of Sorek. Samson loves her and she becomes his mistress, then his wife. She represents the love that diverts the hero from his mission.

2. The Philistines bribe her to discover the source of Samson's extraordinary strength. Delila repeatedly questions Samson, who initially refuses to answer by giving her false explanations, but eventually confesses that his strength comes from his uncut hair, which is the sign of his commitment to God (Judges 16:6, 16:13).

3. Once the secret is discovered, Delila communicates it to the lords of the Philistines who promised her a reward. She puts Samson to sleep, delivers him to his enemies who cut his hair and blind him (Judges 16:18-19). Delila thus becomes the symbol of betrayal and carnal seduction that leads the righteous astray.
H1807.origine: The name Delila means "she who weakens" or "she who is weak" in Hebrew, which is ironic since it is she who weakens Samson. Her name reflects both the image of fragility that she projects to Samson and her true role in his weakening. Although Philistine, she figures in the narrative of the cycle of Samson as a major agent of his downfall.
H1807.emploi: Delila appears only in chapter 16 of the book of Judges, in six occurrences (Judges 16:4, 6, 10, 12, 13, 18). She is first presented as the woman Samson loves (16:4), then becomes the center of the drama when the Philistine leaders contact her to order her to discover the secret of his strength. Delila uses repeated seduction and cunning: she asks Samson to reveal what could bind and subdue him (16:6), then persists when Samson deceives her, until he finally confesses everything to her (16:13-18). Her decisive role in Samson's capture and mutilation makes her one of the most important female figures in the Old Testament, albeit briefly.
H1807.portee: The story of Delila and Samson highlights the danger of carnal seduction that diverts the believer from his commitment to God. Delila represents not so much absolute evil as human fragility in the face of the temptations of the flesh and human love that can lead us away from our faithfulness. Her story warns that human affection, detached from God, can become a weapon of destruction against one who surrenders to it without discernment.

sens: Branch of a tree, lateral shoot that bears leaves and fruits
Branch of a cedar or an olive tree, symbol of strength and natural beauty
Figurative representation of Israel or its leaders, compared to a tree with its branches
H1808.detail:
1. The branch is primarily the branch of a tree: the shoot that grows laterally from the trunk or from other branches, and which bears leaves, flowers, and fruits. It is the living part of the tree that extends towards the sky and provides shade. Ezekiel describes a majestic cedar whose branches spread widely (Ezekiel 31:7).
2. The Bible particularly praises the branches of the cedar and the olive tree, symbols of power, beauty, and fertility. The cedar of Lebanon, the noble tree par excellence, becomes magnificent by the extent and vigor of its branches. The olive tree, with its branches, symbolizes peace and blessing.
3. Figuratively, God compares Israel or its kings to a majestic tree whose branches represent power, greatness, and influence. Jeremiah speaks of the people as a green olive tree whose branches the Lord has broken (Jeremiah 11:16): this is an image of judgment and ruin. Ezekiel uses the branch to show how royal power extends and dominates its enemies (Ezekiel 19:11).
H1808.origine: The Hebrew word דָּלִיּוֹת comes from a root that evokes what hangs, what extends freely. The branch is the natural image of what unfolds from a center (the trunk) outward. This word belongs to a vivid and figurative vocabulary where trees are the favorite comparisons to describe the fate of a people or the power of a king.
H1808.emploi: The word "branch" appears eight times in the Bible, exclusively in the prophetic books of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, always in the plural in French (branches). Jeremiah uses it to depict the misfortune of Israel: the green olive tree burned, its branches broken (Jeremiah 11:16). Ezekiel uses it extensively in allegories about kingdoms: the branches of the cedar that extend (17:23), the vigorous branches that serve as scepters for kings (19:11), or the branches of the majestic cedar that cover the mountains (31:7, 31:9). The branch changes meaning depending on the context: a symbol of blessing and power when it extends, an image of judgment when it is broken or cut off.
H1808.portee: The branch reminds us that power, beauty, and fertility are never permanent. The image of the tree with broken or cut branches warns the believer that God chastises pride and unfaithfulness. Conversely, the vigorous branch that extends under God's protection becomes a promise: under its branches, all that has wings finds rest and security (Ezekiel 17:23). It is an invitation to seek the true source of life, to be planted by God on the high mountain of His will.

sens: To hang, be suspended or balanced, fall low
To be weak, exhausted, weakened
To languish, lack strength or energy
To be in distress, in great moral or physical misery
H1809.detail:
1. In a literal and concrete sense, the word describes something that hangs, is suspended, or balanced downwards. In Job 28:4, the miner "is suspended, balanced, far from humans": he descends into the depths of the earth by ropes.
2. From this comes the idea of being weak, exhausted, without strength. The legs of the lame in Proverbs 26:7 are "weak," unable to carry him properly.
3. The word also expresses languishing, fatigue that removes all vigor. The eyes that languish lose their brightness and ability to see.
4. The Bible uses it primarily in a figurative sense: to be in great distress, crushed by misfortune or suffering. In Judges 6:6, Israel is "very unhappy" under the oppression of Midian, and in the Psalms, one who cries out "I am very unhappy" (Psalms 142:7) describes his deep misery in the face of his enemies.
H1809.origine: The verb first expresses the physical image of something that hangs or sags, hence the sense of weakness and decay. This Hebrew root evokes the movement of falling or lowering. The central idea is that of falling or lowering, which naturally translates to moral and physical states: one who is "unhappy" is downcast, without spring, like something that hangs limply.
H1809.emploi: This verb appears nine times in the Bible. It is used in contexts of national suffering (Israel oppressed by the Midianites in Judges 6:6), personal distress (Psalms 79:8, 116:6, 142:7 where the psalmist confesses his great unhappiness), and also in the physical sense of weakness (the eyes that languish in Isaiah 38:14, the waters that weaken in Isaiah 19:6). The word also applies to moral comparisons: a word in the mouth of a fool is as useless as "the legs of the lame" (Proverbs 26:7). It is a word that unites external and internal distress, physical weakness, and spiritual misery.
H1809.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that distress and unhappiness are never hidden from God. Those who sincerely confess that they are "unhappy" and "languishing" find in God an attentive Savior: "I was unhappy, and He saved me" (Psalms 116:6). The word invites us to acknowledge our weakness and need for help, rather than pretending to have a strength we do not possess.

sens: City of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible
H1810.detail: Dilean is a city in the lowlands of Judah, listed among the cities allocated to the tribe of Judah in the division of the land (Joshua 15:38). Its exact location is uncertain today.
H1810.origine: The name Dilean literally means "gourd" in Hebrew, suggesting a local characteristic: perhaps the city was famous for gourd cultivation, or the name evoked an aspect of the landscape. Like many biblical names, it reflects the environment or a particular feature of the place.
H1810.emploi: Dilean appears only once in the entire Bible, in Joshua 15:38, in the list of cities that the Lord assigned to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of the land of Canaan. It is among the cities of the lowlands, a fertile region in the central-southern part of Judah. The only context in which it is mentioned is administrative and geographical: delineating the territory of Judah and listing the cities that belong to it.

sens: To let tears flow
To weaken, to slacken
To let escape drop by drop
H1811.detail:
1. To let tears flow: the word designates the action of crying, the expression of emotions through tears. It is the most touching image of the verb, that of the heart pouring out. In Job 16:20, Job says that his friends mock him while his eye "cries" to God — his tears rise to heaven like a silent prayer.
2. To weaken, to slacken: the verb can also describe something that sags or loses its firmness, like a structure that gives way. In Ecclesiastes 10:18, when the hands are "slack" (lazy), the house has gutters — the image is that of a house that abandons itself to ruin.
3. To let escape drop by drop: this is the most primitive sense of the word, that of a leak drop by drop, whether it be water or tears. In Psalms 119:28, the soul "cries" in sorrow, as if the tears naturally escape under the weight of pain.
H1811.origine: The verb daleph comes from a root that paints the image of dripping, of trickling. It is a simple and concrete verb, born from observation: a tear that flows, a gutter that leaks. The same root appears in family words to designate what flows or weakens. The sense naturally extends from the physical to the moral: to cry is to let one's emotions escape like water trickling drop by drop.
H1811.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the Bible. In Job 16:20, it evokes the tears of one who suffers and cries out to God. In Psalms 119:28, it describes the soul that melts in tears under the weight of sorrow, asking God to lift it up. In Ecclesiastes 10:18, it moves from the realm of emotions to describe a house that collapses, whose structure sags due to lack of maintenance — here "slack" conveys the idea of hands that relax. It is thus a rare word, concentrated on the expression of suffering and abandonment.
H1811.portee: This verb reminds us that the tears of one who suffers are not hidden from God. They are a form of prayer, a legitimate expression of the wounded heart. The Bible does not ask the believer to hold back their tears, but to direct them to God as to a friend who sees and listens. It is also an invitation not to let oneself go to moral slackness: slack hands bring ruin, as the image in Ecclesiastes reminds us.

sens: That which drips drop by drop, that which trickles
Rain that seeps slowly through a crack or defect in the roof
A quarrelsome woman, whose complaints and disputes are incessant and exhausting
H1812.detail:
1. The word first designates the action of dripping, of flowing drop by drop continuously — a leak of water that flows slowly but steadily.
2. It applies concretely to the gutter or to rain that seeps drop by drop into a building: in Proverbs 27:15, it is compared to "a continuous gutter on a rainy day," the image of a persistent and inevitable flow.
3. Figuratively, the word describes a quarrelsome woman whose complaints and disputes are like those drops that fall endlessly, gnawing and exhausting. It is a crude comparison: just as a leaking gutter makes life impossible for the one who endures it, a woman who constantly disputes ruins the peace of the home (Proverbs 19:13).
H1812.origine: The word comes from a Semitic root that expresses the idea of continuous dripping. The image is that of a persistent water leak, drop by drop. This comparison is never used literally in the Bible: it always serves to figure a moral or relational wound — the woman who tires her husband with her incessant quarrels.
H1812.emploi: The word appears only twice, both in Proverbs, and always applied to a quarrelsome woman. In Proverbs 19:13, a wife's quarrels are presented as "an endless gutter," as harmful and as inevitable as a leak that seeps drop by drop. In Proverbs 27:15, the image sharpens: a "continuous gutter on a rainy day" — that is, a leak that worsens when it rains — is compared to a quarrelsome woman. These two passages use the same metaphor to express weariness, exhaustion, and the impossibility of escaping torment.
H1812.portee: This biblical image shows that words of discord, even if they seem light drop by drop, have a formidable weariness: they slowly but surely gnaw at the peace of the home. It invites everyone to measure the true impact of their repeated words on those who experience them daily, and to seek gentleness rather than constant confrontation.

sens: son of Haman, one of the ten sons of the persecutor of the Jews
H1813.detail: Dalphon is one of the ten sons of Haman, the grand vizier of Xerxes who plotted to exterminate all the Jews of the Persian Empire. After Queen Esther's intervention and the discovery of the plot, Dalphon and his brothers were executed along with their father (Esther 9:7).
H1813.origine: The name Dalphon literally means "that which drips" or "that which oozes." It is a name of Persian origin, like those of his brothers. Its figurative meaning may hint at a physical quality or characteristic, but this remains obscure in the biblical narrative.
H1813.emploi: Dalphon appears only once in the Bible, in Esther 9:7, where he is listed among the ten sons of Haman who were killed. The list of these names in the biblical text holds symbolic significance: it confirms the complete destruction of Haman's household and the fulfillment of divine vengeance after the thwarting of the plot against the Jews.

sens: To burn, to be on fire
To pursue someone relentlessly
To be ardent, passionate, intense
H1814.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to burn or to be on fire: the psalmist's arrows are "burning" (Psalms 7:14), and the fire burns under the pot (Ezekiel 24:10). It is the image of a heat that consumes.
2. On this image of fire is added the idea of pursuing someone with fervor and passion, as one chases an animal or an enemy: Jacob reproaches Laban for "pursuing" him with such ardor (Genesis 31:36), and in Lamentations 4:19, the persecutors "pursue" the people on the mountains — it is a burning, tireless pursuit.
3. The word also designates any emotional or physical intensity: the "burning" lips of a wicked person (Proverbs 26:23) are passionate and evil, and the one who runs after wine in the morning is "heated" by it (Isaiah 5:11) — his desire consumes him.
H1814.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that first evokes the fire that burns, then everything that is ardent or vehement. The heat of fire is the master image: from there comes the idea of passion that drives one to act relentlessly, of fierce pursuit, of desire that ignites. Aramaic uses the same word with the same meaning.
H1814.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, Proverbs, and poetic books. It primarily denotes a physical action: pursuing an enemy or a fugitive (Genesis 31:36, Lamentations 4:19). But the Bible also uses it figuratively to describe a consuming passion: the desire for wine that heats a man (Isaiah 5:11), the malice that burns a wicked person (Proverbs 26:23). The context always shows an intensity, an unrestrained fervor — whether it be the heat of fire, the fervor of a pursuit, or the fire of desire.
H1814.portee: This word reminds readers that human passion — whether vengeance, covetousness, or malice — is a heat that consumes the one who nurtures it. For the psalmist and the prophet, it is also a call to see how only God controls the fire: it warns us against our own destructive fervors and invites us to seek a passion that comes from Him rather than from our own fires.

sens: Flame or fire that burns intensely
Bright glow and heat of fire
Fervor, passionate intensity
H1815.detail:
1. The word describes a fire that burns brightly, with intense flames. In Daniel 7:9, the wheels of the divine throne are compared to a "burning" fire: they radiate a brilliant light and heat, manifesting God's power and glory.
2. The image evokes not only destruction by fire but also its dazzling brilliance. It is the brightness of fire in action — fire as a visible and radiant force, capable of consuming and transforming.
3. In a broader sense, the word can denote intense fervor, a burning passion, the image of fire expressing an energy or intensity that consumes.
H1815.origine: The Aramaic word דְּלַק (delaq) comes from the Hebrew verb דָּלַק (dalaq, H1814), which literally means "to burn" or "to ignite." It belongs to a family of words related to combustion, to fire that devours or radiates. The Hebrew verb expresses both the action of burning and the idea of actively pursuing — two images that share a notion of intensity and rapid movement.
H1815.emploi: This word appears only once in the Aramaic Bible, in Daniel 7:9, where the prophet describes his vision of the throne of the Ancient of Days. The wheels of the throne are described as "a burning fire" — a bright and perpetual flame. It is a context of celestial vision, where the burning fire signifies the holiness, power, and unchanging glory of God. The unique use of the word in this majestic passage underscores its importance in expressing the absolute intensity of the divine presence.
H1815.portee: This word reminds us that God does not reveal Himself in an ordinary or diluted manner. His throne and presence are described with images of burning fire, a symbol of powerful holiness and judgment. For the believer, this invites a reverent fear of God and recognition that His glory consumes and purifies — a call to reverence before the One whose presence is eternal and inexhaustible.

sens: Skin disease characterized by redness, heat, and swelling
Fever or internal fire that consumes the body
Figuratively: divine punishment that burns and destroys
H1816.detail:
1. Inflammation is a visible skin disease, which reddens and heats the affected area. It is a burn or infection that inflames the body, as when a wound becomes infected and becomes hot and swollen.
2. The word can also refer to an intense fever or an internal fire that ravages the body and gradually consumes it, weakening the sufferer.
3. In the context of divine punishment (Deuteronomy 28:22), inflammation appears as one of the calamities that God sends to punish unfaithfulness: it burns and destroys like fire, signifying the divine wrath that falls upon the people.
H1816.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to burn" or "to be ignited," evoking the image of fire. It is the same root found in words designating heat, embers, or blazing. Inflammation is thus literally what "burns" in the body.
H1816.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 28:22, where Moses lists the plagues and diseases that God will send upon Israel if they violate His covenant. Inflammation is included among other scourges (fever, consumption, gangrene) that illustrate the severity of the punishment. It symbolizes the destructive action of divine wrath: a malady that burns, progressively destroys, and ultimately leads to death.
H1816.portee: This passage reminds us that illness and suffering can be calls to repentance. The enumeration of the plagues shows that God never strikes without reason: He warns His people before judging them. For the believer, it is an invitation to take the covenant with God seriously and not to neglect the signs of His warning.

sens: opening allowing entry and exit
access, passage
threshold, entrance to a place
(figurative) lips, mouth as a passage for words
H1817A.detail:
1. The door is the opening of a house or a city through which one enters and exits. It is the place where one can cross a barrier to access what lies beyond.
2. The word also refers to the access or passage itself — the hinge point that connects the inside and the outside.
3. The door is the threshold, the physical entry point of a space — often the first obstacle that one crosses to enter.
4. Figuratively, the door becomes the image of the lips or mouth: it is through them that words come out, just as one enters and exits through a door. Psalm 141:3 illustrates this perfectly: "O Lord, set a guard over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips" — the lips are presented as a door that God must guard to prevent harmful words from escaping.
H1817A.origine: The Hebrew word דָּל (dal) literally refers to the door of a dwelling or a city. This image of passage and entry is very ancient in Semitic languages. The door is naturally the place where a guard stands, hence the figurative use: if one "sets a guard" at the door of their lips, they control what comes out, just as a doorkeeper controls who enters and exits.
H1817A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible with this precise spelling, in Psalm 141:3, in a prayer of David. Here, the psalmist asks God to grant him the gift of restraint: it is not enough to have a physical door; God himself must "guard" it so that foolish, wicked, or hasty words do not escape. It is a plea for divine help to master one's tongue — one of the great themes of biblical wisdom.
H1817A.portee: This image of the door of the lips reminds Christians that words are powerful and need to be guarded. Entrusting the Lord with the guarding of our mouth is to acknowledge that without His help, we speak too much, poorly, or too quickly. This passage invites prayer for discernment in our words and wisdom to say only what builds up.

sens: opening for entry or closure of a room or building
figuratively, that which allows for hiding or protection
H1817B.detail: 1. The door is the opening through which one enters a room or a house, and which can be closed. It is the main access point, the one that is operated to isolate oneself from the outside world. In Isaiah 26:20, the prophet speaks of closing the door of his chamber as a concrete gesture to withdraw and take refuge. 2. Figuratively, the door becomes the image of what protects and conceals us. Closing the door means withdrawing from the world, escaping danger or the approaching storm. In this same verse, it is a call to take refuge internally while the wrath of God passes, just as one hides behind a closed door.
H1817B.origine: The Hebrew word dalah comes from a root that refers to the idea of closure and separation. It designates the simplest constructive element: that which separates the inside from the outside, the private space from the public world. The door is essentially the place of passage and delimitation.
H1817B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 26:20. The prophet uses it poetically and metaphorically to encourage the people to withdraw into intimacy, like in a room whose door is closed, while waiting for divine judgment to pass. The image evokes both physical protection and spiritual refuge, a necessary moment of isolation before deliverance.
H1817B.portee: This passage invites the believer to contemplative prayer and withdrawal from the noise of the world to focus on their relationship with God in times of crisis. Closing the door symbolizes intimacy with God and the trust that, even when hidden, one is protected. It is a powerful image of faith that withdraws to better cling to the Lord.

sens: Opening of a building or enclosure through which one enters and exits
Leaf or panel that closes this opening
Entrance to a city or fortress, usually flanked by towers
Figuratively: that which opens or closes, like a passage
Figuratively: access, occasion or opportunity
Figuratively: the jaws or mouth of an animal
H1817C.detail:
1. The door is the opening made in the wall of a house or enclosure for entering and exiting. It can be opened or closed (Genesis 19:6: Lot "shut the door behind him").
2. The leaf or panel is the movable part, usually made of wood, that pivots on its hinges to close or open access. The Bible mentions these golden leaves in the temple (2 Chronicles 4:22).
3. The door of a city or fortress is its main entry point, often reinforced and guarded, which can be "set" during construction (Nehemiah 6:1: "I had not yet set the doors' leaves").
4. By extension, the door can refer to any passage that opens and closes: figuratively, the "windows of heaven" are the openings through which God sends rain (Psalm 78:23).
5. The door represents access or opportunity: one who listens to wisdom "watches daily at my gates" (Proverbs 8:34), meaning they are on the lookout for the opportunity to draw near.
6. Figuratively, the jaws of a crocodile or the mouth of an animal are compared to doors that close (Job 41:5).
H1817C.origine: The Hebrew word דֶּלֶת (dèlet) comes from a root that evokes what closes, what protects by occlusion. There are few other words in the same family in Hebrew, but the concept remains fundamental: the door is the interface between the inside and the outside, the threshold of home and city. It is a very common word, used both literally and figuratively throughout the Hebrew Bible.
H1817C.emploi: The word דֶּלֶת appears 76 times in the Old Testament, widely distributed across all historical, wisdom, and prophetic books. Literally, it first refers to the door of a house (Genesis 19:6), then the doors of cities (Judges 16:3: Samson carries away the gates of Gaza), the doors of the temple (2 Chronicles 4:22), and the doors of walls (Nehemiah 6:1). Figuratively, the door becomes a symbol: the jaws of the crocodile (Job 41:5), the windows of heaven from which rain comes (Psalm 78:23), or access to wisdom (Proverbs 8:34). The word also applies to what closes: the lid of a chest (Ecclesiastes 12:6), the mouth of an animal. Thus, the door, in biblical Hebrew, is never a simple object: it always represents a threshold, a limit, a guard.
H1817C.portee: The door reminds the reader that God controls the passages and thresholds of life: it can close to protect (Genesis 19:6) or open to grant (Psalm 78:23). Being attentive to the doors of wisdom means remaining vigilant and receptive to God's teaching. The door also illustrates that our life has limits and passages: it is an invitation to guard our accesses with discernment.

sens: Vital red liquid that circulates in the body
Murder, violent death, guilt of spilled blood
Flesh and life of a creature offered in sacrifice
Wine, figure of the color or nature of wine
Descendants, family ties and genealogy
Violent person, murderer or assassin
H1818.detail: 1. Blood is the liquid that gives life to the body: this is why in Genesis 4:10, Abel's blood crying out from the ground represents his life unjustly taken. 2. Spilled blood speaks of murder and guilt: in Genesis 37:22 and 37:26, Joseph's brothers avoid spilling his blood, meaning they do not kill him. The term "bloodthirsty" (2 Samuel 21:1) describes one who has committed murders. 3. In sacrifices, the blood of the offered animal — calf, sheep, goat, bird — represents the life given to God for the forgiveness of sins: it is poured out on the altar (Numbers 18:17) or applied to the penitent (Leviticus 14:14). 4. In Genesis 49:11, "the blood of grapes" is a poetic image of red wine, reminiscent of wine by its color. 5. In "the firstborn of the ox" (Numbers 18:17), blood also evokes life and sacrificed descendants. 6. A "man of blood" (Psalms 139:19) or a "bloody city" (Ezekiel 22:2) refers to one who kills, who sheds the blood of the innocent.
H1818.origine: The Hebrew word dam primarily denotes the living red liquid, hence its natural imagery: life that flows. In Hebrew, blood is linked to life itself ("the life is in the blood," Leviticus 17:11). The word has no clear root in ancient Hebrew, but it is universal in Semitic languages with the same meaning. When speaking of "shedding blood" or "crying out blood," this vital force is personified.
H1818.emploi: The word dam appears 295 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Pentateuch and the Psalms. It primarily refers to the actual blood of animals sacrificed in Levitical rituals: sprinkling, application, offering for forgiveness (Leviticus 1:5, 4:6, 8:15, etc.). It also speaks of committed murder: Abel's blood crying out for vengeance (Genesis 4:10), the intent to kill represented by shedding blood (Genesis 37:22). Finally, it figures wine (Genesis 49:11) or designates murderers by the expression "men of blood" (Psalms 139:19).
H1818.portee: Blood teaches the believer that life comes from God and has a price. The bloody sacrifice of the Old Testament foreshadows the offering of Christ "whose blood was shed for the remission of sins" (Matthew 26:28). It is through blood — in the figurative sense of total self-offering — that one enters into covenant with God. Innocently shed blood cries out for justice: it reminds us that God does not tolerate murder and hears the cry of the oppressed.

sens: To have the appearance or traits of another thing
To be comparable, of the same nature or value
To put oneself in the place of, to imagine
To become similar to, to imitate
H1819.detail:
1. To have the appearance or traits of another thing: this is physical or visible resemblance. "Man is like a breath" (Psalms 144:4): man has the fragile and fleeting appearance of the wind. "Your stature resembles a palm tree" (Song of Solomon 7:8): her silhouette has the graceful height of the palm.
2. To be comparable, of the same nature or value: this goes beyond appearance; it is an equality of rank or power. God asks: "To whom will you compare me, that I should be his equal?" (Isaiah 46:5). No creature is comparable to Him.
3. To put oneself in the place of, to imagine: this is an act of the mind that conceives or thinks something. "We think of your goodness" (Psalms 48:10): the mind represents, contemplates. "God thought it evil" (Psalms 50:21): He had formed the intention.
4. To become similar to, to imitate: this is an act of will that seeks to reproduce the model. Satan says: "I will be like the Most High" (Isaiah 14:14), he wants to make himself equal to God through rebellion.
H1819.origine: The Hebrew verb דָּמָה comes from a root that evokes the image, form, idea of resemblance or representation. The family of this word includes דְּמוּת (form, likeness), from which comes the idea of "figure" or "image." Resemblance is first what one sees, then what one mentally compares, and finally what one imitates. This progression from the concrete (visible aspect) to the abstract (mental comparison) is typical of Hebrew thought.
H1819.emploi: This verb appears 28 times in the Old Testament, mainly in poetry (Psalms, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Ezekiel). In the sense of "to resemble" physically, it compares the beloved's body to elements of nature (Song of Solomon 1:9, 2:9, 7:8). In the sense of "to compare" or "to be equal to," it appears in affirmations of divine power and its incomparability (Isaiah 40:18, 40:25, 46:5). In the sense of "to think, to represent, to imagine," it describes the thoughts of God or humans (Psalms 48:10, 50:21, Isaiah 10:7). In the sense of "to become similar," it expresses Lucifer's proud will (Isaiah 14:14). Each use refines the primary meaning: from visible resemblance to spiritual resemblance.
H1819.portee: This word illuminates how man, created in the image of God, should meditate on this divine resemblance that constitutes him. It also shows the danger of wanting to become like God through rebellion rather than obedience — the path of Lucifer. Through this word, the Bible teaches that true resemblance to God is not a proud conquest, but a grace received and cultivated through conversion and faith.

sens: To stop, come to an end, no longer continue
To be annihilated, disappear, be destroyed
To cause the end of something, destroy, abolish
To be cut off, slain, put to death
To lose strength or consciousness in the presence of a divine manifestation
H1820.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the verb is "to stop," "to cease": something that is going to become still or come to an end. In Jeremiah 14:17, the prophet's tears "do not cease" — they flow uninterruptedly, without stopping their course.
2. When it concerns a person or a city, "to cease" becomes "to be annihilated" or "to be destroyed": to cease to exist. Isaiah 15:1 announces that Moab will be "destroyed" — the city will be annihilated, it will disappear.
3. The verb can also mean "to make cease," that is, "to destroy," "to abolish" actively: the one who acts destroys, removes, annihilates their target.
4. When used in the passive or reflexive form, it denotes the act of being "slain," cut off, killed — like a beast that is slaughtered (Psalms 49:13 and 49:21: the foolish man is "like the beasts that are slaughtered").
5. In the presence of God in His majesty, the verb takes on a religious tone: Isaiah 6:5, before the King of hosts, the prophet cries, "I am lost" — he feels annihilated, reduced to nothing by the holiness of God.
H1820.origine: The root word דָּמָה comes from the idea of "becoming silent" or "making silence," hence the image of "ceasing," "coming to an end." This Hebrew root expresses an interruption, a pause, an annihilation. It likely has links to the idea of becoming similar to something (hence also a sense of "to resemble" in other uses) — but here it focuses on the aspect of destruction or cessation. The family of the word carries the fundamental idea of rupture, interruption, end.
H1820.emploi: The verb דָּמָה appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea, Lamentations, Obadiah, Zephaniah. In Isaiah and Jeremiah, it is used to announce the destruction of cities and peoples (Moab, Gaza, etc.), expressing an inevitable divine judgment. In the Psalms (49:13, 49:21), it compares the foolish man to the beasts "that are slaughtered," emphasizing that wealth and honors do not save from death. In Jeremiah 14:17, the prophet uses it literally to say that his tears do not "cease." The meaning thus varies between "to cease" (intransitive action), "to be destroyed" (passive), "to destroy" (active), and "to slay" or "to kill" — all meanings converge on the idea of an end, destruction, an irrevocable interruption.
H1820.portee: This word reminds us that divine judgment is real and that nothing opposing God endures — empires, cities, human projects without God "cease" and are "destroyed." For the believer, it invites not to place trust in earthly wealth or prestige, which disappear like a slaughtered beast. It also teaches humility in the face of God's holiness: recognizing oneself as "lost" (Isaiah 6:5) before His majesty is the path to repentance and grace.

sens: To have the appearance of something or someone
To be similar in form or aspect
H1821.detail:
1. To have the appearance of something or someone: this verb expresses a visual resemblance, a similarity in appearance. In Daniel 3:25, Nebuchadnezzar sees four men in the fire and says that "the appearance of the fourth is like that of a son of the gods" — he recognizes a resemblance in appearance without asserting identity.

2. To be similar in form or aspect: the word describes a general resemblance, a comparison between two things. In Daniel 7:5, Daniel's vision shows "a second beast resembling a bear" — the beast has the form and look of a bear, even though it remains a prophetic creature.
H1821.origine: This Aramaic verb comes from the same Hebrew root דָּמָה (damah, H1819), which means "to resemble" or "to be similar." The root evokes the idea of resemblance, of similarity in appearance. It belongs to the same family of words as דְּמוּת (demut), "image" or "likeness," and דָּמִי (dami), "similar." In both Aramaic and Hebrew, this verb paints the image of a visual comparison.
H1821.emploi: This verb appears only twice in biblical Aramaic, in the book of Daniel, in chapters 3 and 7. In Daniel 3:25, it describes the resemblance of a divine figure in the fire; in Daniel 7:5, it introduces a prophetic beast compared to a bear. In both cases, the verb establishes a comparison, a striking resemblance that helps the reader grasp a vision. The context is always that of vision or visual perception.
H1821.portee: This word invites the reader to pay attention to what is seen and understood. For Nebuchadnezzar, perceiving a resemblance — that of the fourth figure to a son of the gods — marks the beginning of his recognition of a supernatural presence. The resemblance is never superficial: it opens the eyes and heart to hidden reality.

sens: State of what is annihilated, reduced to nothing
Complete annihilation, disappearance
State of silence and abandonment that follows ruin
H1822.detail: 1. Destruction is the final state of what has been completely annihilated. In Ezekiel 27:32, Tyre, the great trading city, is compared to something "destroyed in the midst of the sea": once prosperous and powerful, it is reduced to nothing, silent, vanished from human life. 2. The word evokes an annihilation so total that all that remains is silence and forgetfulness. It is the image of a city or power that can no longer be heard, that was sought but no longer exists. 3. This destruction carries a dimension of silence: what was destroyed was also "made mute," as if extinguished from the consciousness and memory of the living.
H1822.origine: The Hebrew word dummah comes from a root that expresses the idea of being silent, still, or stifled. It is formed to designate the state of one who is rendered silent by force, death, or annihilation. This root belongs to the field of Hebrew words describing silence and stillness, often related to death or the end.
H1822.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:32, at the heart of a prophetic lamentation over the ruin of Tyre. Ezekiel, the prophet, imagines how the sailors and merchants who once saw this powerful city will lament when it is destroyed: "Who was like Tyre, like that city destroyed in the midst of the sea?" The context is that of divine judgment on a proud and wealthy city, which will suddenly be reduced to nothing. The word emphasizes both the physical annihilation and the silence that results: Tyre will be nothing but a mute ruin.
H1822.portee: This word reminds the reader that even the greatest human powers, even the richest and most influential cities, can be reduced to nothing by the judgment of God. It invites reflection on the vanity of earthly riches and the fragility of all that opposes God. The silence that envelops destruction is also a warning: a civilization can disappear so completely that its past existence is forgotten.

sens: What makes two things similar, their common point
The outward appearance of a person or thing
The shape, general appearance of an object
What imitates or reproduces a model
H1823.detail:
1. What makes two things similar, their common point: it is the trait or set of traits they share. When God creates man "in our image, according to our likeness" (Genesis 1:26), He establishes a relationship of similarity between man and God — man bears the mark of the divine in his nature. It is also what makes two beings or objects resemble each other in their structure.
2. The outward appearance of a person or thing: what is seen when looking. In Ezekiel's visions, the heavenly creatures "had a human likeness" (Ezekiel 1:5), meaning they presented the appearance of human beings, even though their nature was entirely different.
3. The shape, general appearance of an object: its lines, silhouette. When Ahaz receives from the prophet Uriah the exact model of an altar (2 Kings 16:10), he obtains a plan that reproduces point by point its shape and dimensions — the likeness must be perfect.
4. What imitates or reproduces a model: a copy, a faithful representation. The word often designates in the Bible images or figures that make visible what is invisible or distant, such as the forms of creatures in prophetic visions.
H1823.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to resemble" or "to be alike." It is constructed with the abstract noun suffix that transforms the action into a general idea: of the likeness itself, rather than the simple verb "to resemble." This root appears in several words of the same family that all evoke similarity, comparison, or imitation. It is a fundamental word in biblical thought to express the link of conformity that unites things with each other or a creature to its model.
H1823.emploi: The word appears 22 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the prophet Ezekiel (13 occurrences), who uses it to describe his heavenly visions — the creatures, thrones, wheels he contemplates. In the Pentateuch, it appears in relation to man created in the image of God (Genesis 1:26; 5:1; 5:3). The uses of the word show that "likeness" can denote either an abstract and spiritual resemblance — that which binds man to God — or a visible and descriptive resemblance — that which is observed in appearances and forms. Particularly in Ezekiel, it is the key word to show that even supernatural beings are seen by the prophet in a form that makes them intelligible: they have a likeness to known things (humans, animal creatures, objects), which allows the prophet to describe them. The word can also denote an exact imitation, a reproduced model (2 Kings 16:10).
H1823.portee: This word reminds the reader that man is created in the likeness of God — this establishes his dignity and responsibility. It indicates that the relationship of man to God is not arbitrary: it rests on a conformity inscribed in his very nature. When the prophet Ezekiel uses "likeness" to describe heavenly visions, he teaches us that even the invisible can become visible, provided we accept that God descends, in a sense, to our human categories to make Himself intelligible. It is a word that speaks of both dignity (for man) and pedagogical humility (for God who deigns to be seen).

sens: silence, mutism
inaction, suspension of activity
calm, peace, tranquility
respite, temporary relief
H1824.detail:
1. Silence or mutism — the act of not speaking, remaining silent. In Psalm 83:2, the psalmist pleads with God: "Do not remain silent! Do not be quiet"; here, domi refers to the absence of speech, the inactivity of one who is silent.

2. Inaction, rest, or suspension — the interruption of an activity, the state of one who ceases to work or act. Isaiah 38:10 uses it for the days when life stops, when one enters the rest of death: "When my days are in rest, I must depart."

3. Calm and inner peace — the tranquility that comes when one ceases to be agitated or to struggle. It is a state of relaxation and serenity.

4. Respite or relief — a temporary suspension of something that weighs or tires. Isaiah 62:6-7 gives the image: the watchmen of Jerusalem "will not be silent day or night" and will give God "no rest" until He restores the city; here, domi is the stopping of the cry, the cessation of importunity.
H1824.origine: The Hebrew word domi comes from a root that means "to be silent, to be quiet, to keep silent." It is related to the adjective "mute" and the verb "to be silent." The initial image is that of silence, the absence of noise or speech. It has broadened to encompass all cessation, all rest, and all inaction, as if silence were the first sign of peace.
H1824.emploi: This word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, only in Psalms and Isaiah. In Psalm 83:2, it refers to the silence of God, perceived as a painful absence. In Isaiah 38:10, it describes the quiet days when life gradually stops. In Isaiah 62:6-7, it takes on the meaning of a relief or cessation: the intercessors do not give God rest, meaning they do not cease to plead. The religious context is constant: it concerns the relationship between man and God, between prayer and divine silence.
H1824.portee: This word reminds the believer that God's silence is never indifference, and that one should not abandon prayer out of fatigue or impatience. It also teaches that true rest comes from God alone, not from our efforts, and that the peace He gives surpasses the agitation of the world. Finally, it shows that persevering in prayer is to deny God Himself the right to remain silent, and it is the highest form of trust in His goodness.

sens: To have the appearance of, to resemble
To seem, to appear
H1825.detail:
1. This word describes a resemblance or similarity between two things: something has the aspect, look, or air of something else. In Psalm 17:12, the psalmist describes his enemy and says that he "would say" a lion — meaning he resembles a lion, that he has the threatening look of a lion on the prowl. The image is of a person whose behavior and appearance suggest a dangerous beast.
2. More broadly, the word expresses the impression, the appearance as it presents itself: one does not say "it is," but "it would seem," "it appears." It is the contrast between objective reality and the impression it gives. It is a word of analogy, not identity: the enemy is not a lion, but he has the threatening aspect of one.
H1825.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that carries the idea of comparison and resemblance. Its meaning rests on the image of what resembles, what has the same form or aspect. In biblical Hebrew, this type of word served to express analogies, images, and comparisons — essential tools of biblical poetry and wisdom.
H1825.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 17:12. It is in a context of supplication: the psalmist, confronted by enemies who are pursuing him, describes them in terrifying terms — they resemble predators. It is a poetic image to express the mortal danger and destructive intent of those who pursue him. The context shows that the enemy acts with the ferocity of a wild beast.
H1825.portee: For the believer reading this psalm, this word reminds that the threats of evil take terrifying forms and seem overwhelming. But it is precisely in these moments when one cries out to God that faith takes refuge in Him. The psalmist does not question whether the danger is real; he asks God to save him from what threatens him — a lesson in trust despite fear.

sens: to remain mute, unable to speak
to cease moving, to stop
to persist without interruption
to passively accept, to wait without acting
H1826A.detail:
1. To be struck dumb or unable to speak: it is the image of a person or thing rendered mute by fear, terror, or helplessness. In Exodus 15:16, the enemies of Israel "will become mute like a stone" in the face of God's wonders, unable to react.
2. To stop, to cease movement: it is to immobilize something in motion. The sun and the moon "stop" at the voice of Joshua (Joshua 10:12-13), suspending their usual course to prolong the day of battle.
3. To continue without respite, to persevere: when speaking of something that endures "without ceasing," it is a state that does not interrupt. Job describes his sufferings that boil without "ceasing" (Job 30:27), and the oppressed is torn without "ceasing" (Psalms 35:15).
4. To passively accept, to remain inactive: it is to keep silent, to wait without intervening. In 1 Samuel 14:9, "stop" means to stay in place and let things happen.
H1826A.origine: The root fundamentally means "to remain still and silent." It evokes the image of complete cessation: stopping noise, stopping movement, stopping action. The word can refer to both physical silence and immobility, often linked in experience: one who is paralyzed by fear becomes mute and frozen.
H1826A.emploi: The verb appears 9 times in the Old Testament, mostly in dramatic contexts. In Exodus and Joshua, it describes miraculous stops or paralysis in the face of God's power. In Job and Psalms, it characterizes persistent and unbroken sufferings ("without ceasing"). In 1 Samuel, it denotes a tactical pause. In Jeremiah and Lamentations, it invites to passive abandonment, to cease complaint or resistance. The meaning thus varies according to the context: sudden immobility, imposed silence, persistence of pain, or resignation.
H1826A.portee: This word reminds the reader that silence is not always weakness: before God, it is wisdom. It also teaches that relentless suffering may seem infinite, but it will have its end. For the believer, being silent before God is a form of obedience and trust, accepting His ways without murmuring.

sens: To remain silent in astonishment or terror
To be quiet under the weight of overwhelming emotion
To lose one's words in the face of the unimaginable
H1826B.detail: 1. The verb primarily expresses a complete silence, but not an ordinary one: it is the silence that cannot be broken, that of one who is struck with astonishment. In Isaiah 23:2, the inhabitants of the coast and the merchants are called to be silent with fear upon learning of the ruin of Sidon: their prosperous trade collapses, and this catastrophe paralyzes them so completely that they cannot even find words to lament it. 2. It is a silence that denounces the extent of the shock: one cannot speak, not by choice, but because terror or desolation has sealed one's lips. This involuntary muteness says more than screams — it shows that the event exceeds all expression.
H1826B.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the absence of sound, the soundless void. It is related to words meaning "silence" and "tranquility," but in a context of overwhelming emotion, it takes on a dramatic hue: it is not the peaceful silence of rest, but the forced mutism of one who is devastated.
H1826B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 23:2. There, the prophet announces God's judgment against Sidon and its prosperous maritime trade. The command "Be silent with fear" is addressed to the coastal inhabitants: they must understand that their wealth and power do not protect them from ruin. The fear spoken of by Isaiah is not a mere fleeting fear; it is the shock of a terrible revelation, that of human helplessness in the face of divine decrees.
H1826B.portee: This word reminds us that in the face of God's sovereign acts, human words become useless. There are moments when humble silence is the only appropriate response to divine majesty and justice. For the Christian, this can inspire an awe-filled reverence before God, a recognition that our plans and riches are fragile.

sens: To remain silent, to say nothing
To remain still, calm, without agitation
To be paralyzed by fear, unable to speak
To lose one's voice, to become mute
To die, to cease to live
To be destroyed, annihilated
H1826H.detail:
1. To remain silent means to close one's mouth and not speak. This is what Aaron does before the death of his sons: he "kept silent" (Leviticus 10:3), accepting without protest God's judgment. It is also what the psalmist asks of his heart: "do not be silent" (Psalms 30:13), so that he can sing and praise God.
2. To remain still and calm means to wait without moving, to accept the situation. The psalmist says: "trust in God," which implies remaining quiet, not agitated by worry (Psalms 62:6).
3. To be paralyzed by fear means to lose the use of speech under the effect of terror. Job confesses: "I was afraid... not daring to cross my door" (Job 31:34), as if fear sealed his mouth and legs.
4. To become mute is to lose the ability to speak, either through illness or divine intervention. The psalmist fears that his heart may become mute, meaning incapable of celebrating God.
5. To die or perish describes the end of life. In Jeremiah 50:30, it is written: "all her warriors will perish that day." The silence of death replaces the noise of life.
6. To be destroyed or annihilated means to disappear completely. Jeremiah announces: "Madmen, you shall be destroyed" (Jeremiah 48:2), meaning erased from the map.
H1826H.origine: The Hebrew verb דָּמַם (damam) primarily describes the idea of remaining without noise, becoming inert. Its root evokes calm, the absence of movement and sound. The word belongs to a family of Hebrew terms related to silence and stillness. In biblical Hebrew, it expresses both voluntary rest and forced immobility — that caused by fear, death, or destruction. It is a word that captures the moment when life stops, when noise ceases.
H1826H.emploi: This verb appears about fifteen times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and among the prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel. It first describes a voluntary silence: Aaron keeps silent before God (Leviticus 10:3), or the believer calms himself in silence to trust (Psalms 62:6, Psalms 4:5). Then it takes on graver meanings: paralysis by fear (Job 31:34), muteness (Psalms 30:13), and finally destruction or death during divine judgment (Jeremiah 48:2, Jeremiah 50:30). In Lamentations, it is the painful silence of those who weep (Lamentations 2:10, Lamentations 3:28).
H1826H.portee: This word teaches the Christian that silence is not always an absence, but sometimes a presence: that of trust in God, of listening, of humble acceptance. Aaron kept silent because he understood that God was acting justly. But damam also shows that allowing God to speak sometimes requires renouncing our words, our agitation, our defenses — a call to inner peace and submission.

sens: To be destroyed, annihilated, to disappear
To be rendered silent, immobilized
To undergo death, to succumb
H1826I.detail:
1. To perish means to be completely destroyed or annihilated. It conveys the idea of a violent and definitive end. In 1 Samuel 2:9, the wicked "will be annihilated in darkness": they disappear, engulfed by God's judgments. In Jeremiah 25:37, the "peaceful dwellings are destroyed" by the Lord's anger — everything is ruined, reduced to nothing.
2. The word also evokes the idea of being rendered silent or immobilized, as if death itself freezes you. It is a destruction that paralyzes.
3. To perish also means to die, to succumb in the face of an irresistible force. In Jeremiah 8:14, the people say, "let us go to the fortified cities, to perish there" — aware that they are heading to their own death. In Jeremiah 51:6, they cry, "flee from Babylon... lest you perish in her ruin" — risking death in the catastrophe.
H1826I.origine: The Hebrew verb דָּמַם (damam) comes from a root that evokes silence and immobility. It appears in several forms: "to be silent" is the main meaning, but silence leads to immobility, then to death — for one who no longer speaks, who no longer moves, is annihilated. The word can also mean "to be struck dumb" or "to be rendered mute." The family of the word expresses everywhere this idea of reduction, suppression, end.
H1826I.emploi: This verb appears 4 times in the provided usages, all in Jeremiah and 1 Samuel. It always describes a destruction or death imposed by God or by the force of events. In 1 Samuel 2:9, it is the annihilation of the wicked — a divine judgment. In Jeremiah 8:14, the people acknowledge their fate of death. In Jeremiah 25:37 and 51:6, it is the destruction of cities and dwellings by God's judgments, particularly against Babylon. The word always emphasizes a character of inevitability and totality: nothing escapes.
H1826I.portee: This word reminds us that God's judgments are real and irrevocable. There is no salvation for one who persists in rebellion — eternal silence, annihilation, is the fate of those who reject God. For the believer, it is also a call not to remain indifferent in the face of divine wrath: one must "flee" (as in Jeremiah 51:6) and turn to God to live.

sens: A very soft and barely perceptible sound, almost a whisper
A voice that speaks softly, without force or brilliance
The calm that follows agitation, the tranquility regained
H1827.detail: 1.
