The gentle whisper is a sound that is barely heard, like a breath or a whisper: this is how the prophet Elijah hears the voice of God, not in the earthquake or in the fire, but in this gentle and quiet whisper (1 Kings 19:12). 2. It can also be a voice that speaks softly, without shouting, like the one Job hears coming from a mysterious figure (Job 4:16): not a thunderous word, but something confidential, intimate. 3. Figuratively, this word also designates calm itself, the peace that replaces disorder: when the Lord stills a storm and brings calm over the troubled waters, it is this whisper, this regained tranquility, that soothes the waves (Psalms 107:29).
H1827.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of what is gentle, light, tranquil. It is composed of reduplication (two times the same syllable), which in the Hebrew language often reinforces the idea: the gentle whisper is truly very light, very soft. The word can designate both the imperceptible sound and the absence of noise, the calm silence.
H1827.emploi: This word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of encounter with the divine or deliverance. In 1 Kings 19, it characterizes the subtle presence of God: it is not in the noisy and spectacular phenomena that the Lord reveals Himself to the prophet, but in what requires listening, silent attention. In Job 4, the whisper accompanies the vision and the word that comes from mystery. In Psalms 107, the same word describes the transformation of the storm into peace: the passage from chaos to rest. Each time, it evokes something that does not impose itself by force, but requires attentiveness.
H1827.portee: This word teaches the reader that the presence and action of God are not always spectacular: often, it is in the whisper, in the calm, in what requires attentive listening that we truly encounter the Lord. It invites to inner peace and trust, reminding that God can still the storms of our lives and bring us back to calm. It is a word for those who seek God not in tumult, but in the attentive silence of the heart.

sens: Excrement or decomposing organic matter
A degrading deposit, without value or dignity
State of dishonor and extreme humiliation
Total destruction and oblivion, without burial or memory
H1828.detail: 1. Manure in the literal sense is fecal matter or organic debris that accumulates. But this Hebrew word never speaks of manure as fertilizer or agricultural resource: it always designates corpses treated with disrespect, thrown away and rotting in the open air, as in 2 Kings 9:37 where Jezebel's body becomes "manure on the face of the fields." 2. Manure is the image of what has no value, no honorable place. Those who die without burial "have become manure for the earth" (Psalms 83:11), treated worse than beasts: they remain exposed, visible, despised. 3. It is a symbol of divine humiliation: those who have rejected God suffer an undignified death. Jeremiah announces that the corpses will be "like manure on the earth, they will neither be lamented, nor gathered, nor buried" (Jeremiah 25:33) — the image concentrates the idea that God removes all dignity from those who have abandoned Him. 4. Finally, it is the ultimate fate: absolute oblivion and annulment. No name, no grave, no memory — just a vile substance that disappears.
H1828.origine: The Hebrew word dōmen comes from a root that evokes the idea of throwing, projecting outside, or perhaps of what lies in a heap. It is never a neutral term: it carries the idea of rejection and defilement. In Hebrew, manure is always an image of contempt and destruction, never an ordinary agricultural reality.
H1828.emploi: The word appears 6 times, all in texts of judgment. In 2 Kings 9:37, it is the fate of Jezebel after her condemnation. In the Psalms (83:11), it is that of the enemies of Israel who are annihilated. But above all, Jeremiah uses it 4 times (8:2, 9:22, 16:4, 25:33) to describe the consequences of divine judgment on Judah: the corpses of the rebels will remain unburied, exposed, denied. It is the ultimate penalty: not only death, but the annulment of all funeral dignity. The word concentrates both the physical horror (the decaying body) and the moral horror (oblivion, absence of memory).
H1828.portee: This word shows the gravity of divine judgment in the Hebrew Bible. For an Israelite, burial was a sacred right; to refuse manure to the corpse is the worst of punishments, for it says: "You count for nothing, you are less than nothing." This reminds us that God takes the rejection of His Word very seriously. But for the believer, this word also shows that a life devoted to God leads to honor, not contempt.

sens: City of the tribe of Levi, in the territory of Zebulun
H1829.detail: Dimna is a city assigned to the Levites, particularly to the tribe of Levi which did not inherit a specific territory in Canaan. It was located within the boundaries of the tribe of Zebulun, in the northern part of the Promised Land. The Bible mentions that this city had a suburb, that is, an area of pastures and common lands around it, intended to feed the livestock of the Levites who lived there. See Joshua 21:35.
H1829.origine: The name Dimna literally means "heap of manure" in Hebrew, probably a reference to the nature of the soil or the appearance of the site. This city is also known by the name Rimmon (a term meaning "pomegranate"), suggesting that it had two names in antiquity, a common practice in Canaan.
H1829.emploi: Dimna appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 21:35, in a list of cities assigned to the Levites after the conquest of Canaan. It is mentioned alongside Nahalal, with their respective suburbs. These Levitical cities served as religious and administrative centers, where the priests and Levites carried out their functions among the people of Israel.

sens: To shed tears, to cry intensely
To let tears flow due to emotion
To express sorrow or compassion through tears
H1830.detail: 1. The verb literally describes the act of crying, especially when tears flow abundantly. The image is of tears that "melt" and flow from the face. In Jeremiah 13:17, God says through the mouth of the prophet: "My eyes will weep bitterly," expressing the depth of His sorrow over Israel's unfaithfulness and the exile that will follow. 2. Beyond the simple act of crying, the word expresses intense emotion: sorrow, compassion, or mourning. It is a weeping that springs from the heart, not a restrained tear. Here, it is the pain of a shepherd — God Himself — who sees His beloved people taken into captivity because of their pride.
H1830.origine: The Hebrew verb דָּמַע (dama) literally means "to weep" or "to shed tears." It is related to the idea of liquid flowing and melting, hence the translation "to melt" in French. The root expresses the concrete image of tears flowing from the face under the weight of emotion.
H1830.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 13:17. It is a word from God addressed to the prophet Jeremiah to rebuke the people of Israel. God expresses here His wounded love and compassion for His flock by announcing their captivity: He will weep in secret over their fate because of their pride. The context shows that this divine weeping manifests both judgment and the love of the Lord.
H1830.portee: This verse reveals God's deep emotion in the face of His people's unfaithfulness. Far from being indifferent or merely angry, God suffers to see those He loves turn away from Him. For the Christian reader, it is a call to understand that God does not distance Himself from evil: He is affected by it, and His correction comes from a heart that loves. It is also an invitation to compassion for those who are lost.

sens: the gathering of cut and collected grains
the entire work and period of the harvest
the moment in the agricultural cycle when the harvest takes place
that which is harvested, the product of the land
H1831.detail:
1. The harvest is primarily the moment when grains (wheat, barley, rye) that have ripened in the fields are cut. In Exodus 22:29, the Lord asks Israel for the firstfruits of the harvest, meaning the first crops, as a sign of gratitude to the Creator.
2. The word also refers to all the work and activity surrounding this harvest: cutting the sheaves, gathering them, binding them. It is an important and demanding period in the life of the farmer.
3. By extension, it designates the season itself, the time of year when the harvest occurs, distinguished from other agricultural tasks such as plowing or sowing.
4. Finally, the word can simply evoke what is harvested: the grain gathered and ready to be used.
H1831.origine: The Hebrew word is derived from a root that evokes the action of cutting or slicing. It is a very concrete image: one cuts the plants from the field. The harvest was a crucial event in an agrarian society, marking the culmination of the work of an entire agricultural cycle.
H1831.emploi: The word appears only once in the provided texts (Exodus 22:29) in a context of religious law. The Lord commands the people of Israel not to delay in offering Him the firstfruits of the harvest: this is the first portion of the crop that must be dedicated to Him, along with the new wine from the vintage. This offering reminded them that the land and its fruits come from God and that the first right belongs to Him. The harvest was eagerly awaited after months of work and sowing, and its success was considered a blessing from Heaven.
H1831.portee: The harvest speaks to the Christian of the culmination of work and the rest that accompanies it. It also symbolizes the fulfillment of God's promises: what He has sown in the believer's heart must bear fruit. Finally, by reminding us to offer the firstfruits to the Lord, it calls the Christian to recognize that all his possessions come from God and that the first right belongs to Him.

sens: A drop of water that flows from the eye
To cry, to shed tears
An expression of sorrow, suffering, or repentance
A mark of divine compassion
H1832.detail:
1. A tear is primarily the physical drop of water that comes from the eye: it is the visible water of crying. In 2 Kings 20:5, Hezekiah weeps upon learning of his serious illness, and the Lord sees his tears.
2. To shed tears means to cry intensely, to let the tears flow freely. Jeremiah 9:1 expresses this desire: "If my eyes were a fountain of tears, I would weep day and night" — the image of an inexhaustible fountain of tears.
3. The tear becomes the tangible sign of deep sorrow, suffering, or sincere repentance. In Psalms 42:4, tears are "my food day and night," in other words: the source of my life becomes my pain. In Lamentations, tears flood the eyes of the prophet who contemplates the ruin of Jerusalem.
4. Tears also have a spiritual significance: they touch the heart of God. Isaiah 25:8 announces that the Lord "will wipe away tears from all faces" on the day of final redemption, revealing that God sees, records, and comforts the weeping of His people.
H1832.origine: The Hebrew word dīm'ah comes from a root that means "to flow" or "to stream." It is related to other terms that denote water or fluids. The word naturally evokes the image of water flowing from the body — here, the source of emotion that comes from the eye. It is a simple and ancient word, rooted in the direct observation of a crying body.
H1832.emploi: The word tear appears 22 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the poetic (Psalms, Lamentations) and prophetic (Jeremiah, Isaiah) books. It is found in three main contexts: first, the supplication of the faithful who cry out to God in suffering (Psalms 6:7, 39:13), then mourning and lamentation over a catastrophe (Lamentations 1:2, 2:11, Jeremiah 14:17), and finally prophetic intercession for the afflicted people (Isaiah 16:9, Jeremiah 9:1). Tears are rarely presented as shame or weakness: on the contrary, they manifest the intensity of the heart before God or reality. The Word also reveals that God "collects" tears (Psalms 56:9), keeps them in a bottle (poetic form), sees them, and responds to them.
H1832.portee: Tears teach us that the emotion of the heart is not contrary to true faith, but is often its deepest expression. When we weep over suffering, sin, or loss, our tears do not go unnoticed: God sees them, counts them, and comforts us. This truth frees the believer from the shame of crying and brings him closer to a God who empathizes and promises, one day, to wipe every tear from our eyes.

sens: A precious and crafted fabric, probably made of silk or fine linen, adorned with patterns
An object of luxury and domestic comfort among the wealthy
H1833.detail:
1. The word refers to a fine and quality fabric, probably made of silk or linen woven with artistry. It is uncertain whether "damask" comes from the name of the city of Damascus (renowned for its weaving) or if it simply describes a pattern — but it is a delicate and valued fabric, likely with designs or motifs that distinguish it. In Amos 3:12, the prophet mentions "damask rugs" to evoke the ease and refinement of the wealthy in Israel who, sitting on their luxurious beds, believe they are secure — while judgment falls upon them. The rug here symbolizes carnal prosperity and false confidence.
2. The damask rug represents material comfort and wealth: it is what one lies on in opulent interiors, far from any concern. It is one of those marks of social status that dulls spiritual vigilance.
H1833.origine: The etymology remains uncertain. Either the word comes from Damascus, the great Syrian city famous since antiquity for its weaving and trade in fine fabrics — and "damask" would have become the generic name for a luxury fabric. Or it derives from a Semitic root denoting a particular weaving technique or a characteristic pattern. The word appears only once in biblical Hebrew, making its genesis difficult to establish with certainty.
H1833.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in Amos 3:12. The prophet Amos uses it in a judgment oracle to stigmatize the insolent luxury of the great ones of Israel. He paints a scene of voluptuous rest — men reclining on beds covered with precious rugs — to contrast with the imminence of disaster. This is not a neutral description: it is a denunciation of attachment to riches and forgetfulness of God. The damask rug embodies here all that prosperity and the idolatry of comfort brought to Israel just before its punishment.
H1833.portee: This word reminds the Christian that material comfort and luxury, in themselves, are not sinful — but they become dangerous when they lull us spiritually and divert us from obedience to God. The damask rug of Amos is an invitation to examine where our trust lies: in our wealth and earthly well-being, or in the Word of the Lord? It is a classic warning of biblical prophecy: prosperity is not a guarantee of spiritual security; it is often a trap.

sens: Ancient capital of Syria, major commercial city of the ancient Near East
Politically and militarily significant center in Mesopotamia
City often in conflict or alliance with the kingdoms of Israel and Judah
H1834.detail:
1. Damascus is a large city located in a plain east of Mount Hermon, about 205 kilometers northeast of Jerusalem. It was an important crossroads of ancient trade, where caravan routes and merchant exchanges passed through (Ezekiel 27:18 mentions it among the cities that prospered through trade).
2. Damascus served as the capital of Syria and the seat of political and military power. Kings of Syria, such as Ben-Hadad, resided there (2 Chronicles 16:2), and the city played a major role in the affairs of the Near East.
3. Throughout biblical history, Damascus has been both an enemy and an ally of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, making it a city of major political stakes (1 Kings 19:15; 2 Kings 16:9 show the conflicts and successive takeovers).
H1834.origine: The name "Damascus" (Hebrew דַּמֶּשֶׂק) traditionally means "silence of the sack weaver," although the exact etymology remains debated among scholars. The name also appears in ancient Akkadian and Egyptian historical sources, attesting to its importance in the ancient world. The city has retained this name through the centuries and still exists today, known in modern Arabic as Damascus.
H1834.emploi: Damascus appears about 40 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the historical books (Kings, Chronicles) and in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos, Ezekiel). The Bible first presents it as a distant city (Genesis 14:15), then as the seat of a formidable rival kingdom. Under the reigns of Ahaz and Manasseh, it plays a decisive role in the wars of Judah (2 Kings 16:9; 2 Chronicles 28:5). The prophets announce its future judgment, particularly Isaiah and Jeremiah, who predict its destruction by Assyria (Isaiah 17:1; Jeremiah 49:27). Amos criticizes it for its oppression (Amos 1:3).
H1834.portee: Damascus symbolizes in the Bible the power of the world that does not recognize the God of Israel. Its prophesied fall reminds us that human kingdoms, no matter how great and rich they may be, are subject to God's judgment. For the believer, this example shows that God governs history and that no earthly kingdom can stand against His will.

sens: Son of Jacob and Bilhah, founder of the tribe of Israel that bears his name
Tribe of Israel descended from Dan
Territory allocated to the tribe of Dan in the Promised Land
Fortified city in northern Canaan, capital of the tribe of Dan
Geographical landmark marking the northern boundary of Israel
H1835G.detail:
1. Dan is the son of Jacob and Bilhah, Leah's maid. His name literally means "he judges," evoking justice and authority. He is one of the twelve patriarchs from whom the tribes of Israel descend (Exodus 1:4).

2. The tribe of Dan is one of the twelve tribes of Israel, with its own military responsibilities and its prince named Ahiezer during the desert (Numbers 2:25). It clearly appears in the census of the people.

3. The territory of Dan in Canaan is assigned to the tribe by lot (Joshua 19:40). However, due to the hostility of the Amorites, the Danites struggle to conquer their share (Judges 1:34) and seek another region.

4. The city of Dan is fortified in the northern part of the Promised Land. It becomes the center of life for the tribe and later the seat of an idolatrous worship established by Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:29-30).

5. "From Dan to Beersheba" becomes a classic formula to designate the complete extent of Israel from north to south, with Dan marking the northernmost boundary (2 Samuel 24:2).
H1835G.origine: Dan comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to judge" or "to govern." Jacob gave this name to his son saying, "God has vindicated me" (Genesis 30:6). The name expresses the idea of an authority that discerns and decides. The tribe and territory that bear this name retain the identity of the founding patriarch, and the city of Dan, established in the north after the conquest of Canaan, becomes the northernmost geographical landmark of the united kingdom of Israel.
H1835G.emploi: Dan appears 57 times in the Hebrew Bible, designating both the patriarch, the tribe, the territory, and the city. It is found in genealogical lists (Exodus 1:4), census in the desert (Numbers 1-2), land allocation (Joshua 19:40-48), and the history of the Judges where the tribe seeks to expand its territory through conquest (Judges 18). The city of Dan becomes famous as the northern landmark of Israel (2 Samuel 24:2) and later as a site of royal idolatrous worship (1 Kings 12:29). Dan also appears in the prophetic visions of Ezekiel regarding the future distribution of territory (Ezekiel 48:1-2).

sens: Son de Jacob et de Bilhah, servante de Rachel
Tribu d'Israël descendue de Dan
Ville ou région du nord de Palestine
H1835H.detail:
1. Dan est le cinquième fils de Jacob, premier enfant qu'il a eu de Bilhah, la servante de Rachel. Son nom signifie « un juge », car Rachel a dit en l'enfantant : « Dieu m'a rendu justice » (Genèse 30:6). Il a un frère utérin, Nephthali, et neuf demi-frères ainsi qu'une demi-sœur nés des autres épouses de Jacob.
2. La tribu de Dan est l'une des douze tribus d'Israël, descendue de Dan fils de Jacob. Elle reçoit l'appel à juger son peuple, mais la bénédiction prophétique la décrit aussi comme rusée et dangereuse, « un serpent sur le chemin » qui mord les talons du cheval pour faire tomber le cavalier (Genèse 49:16-17).
3. Dan désigne aussi une ville du nord de Palestine, qui devient la limite septentrionale du territoire d'Israël, si bien qu'on dit souvent « de Dan à Beersébée » pour désigner toute l'étendue du pays.
H1835H.origine: Le nom hébreu signifie littéralement « il a jugé » ou « un juge ». Rachel l'a choisi pour célébrer le jugement favorable de Dieu envers elle, qui l'avait longtemps privée d'enfants. C'est un nom théophore, qui exprime la reconnaissance envers l'action salvifique de Dieu.
H1835H.emploi: Dan apparaît six fois dans les passages fournis. Il est d'abord nommé comme nouveau-né en Genèse 30:6, puis figuré dans la liste des enfants de Jacob (Genèse 35:25 ; 1 Chroniques 2:2). Son fils Huschim est mentionné en Genèse 46:23. Les deux versets de bénédiction (Genèse 49:16-17) révèlent le caractère et le destin spirituel de la tribu : elle aura un rôle de juge, mais sera aussi confrontée à la tentation de la ruse et de la violence.
H1835H.portee: Dan rappelle au lecteur chrétien que même dans les lignées de l'Ancien Testament, la providence de Dieu ouvre des voies nouvelles : Rachel, autrefois stérile, reçoit des fils et loue le jugement divin. La prophétie sur Dan (tribu et homme) invite aussi à méditer sur le danger de la ruse et de la malveillance, même au sein du peuple de Dieu, et sur l'appel à exercer l'autorité avec justice plutôt que par la sournoiserie.

sens: Designates a person, thing, or situation that is present or immediate
Introduces or highlights what has just been mentioned
Indicates the cause or reason for something
Expresses a conclusion or logical deduction
H1836.detail: 1. The word designates what is close, present, or happening: "this house of God" (Ezra 6:16) or "this writing" traced by the divine hand (Daniel 5:24) point to visible and immediate realities. 2. It introduces or recalls what has just been mentioned, as in Ezra 4:11 where "here is the copy of the letter" refers back to the subject of the previous sentence, or in Daniel 2:28 where it highlights the dream already mentioned. 3. It marks the cause: "on your bed" (Daniel 2:28) or "That is why he sent this writing" (Daniel 5:24) link a consequence to its reason. 4. It can introduce a conclusion or explanation that logically follows from what precedes: Ezra 5:7 "thus conceived" shows how the report is stated following what has come before.
H1836.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the root דנ, which expresses the idea of showing, pointing out. It belongs to the family of Aramaic demonstratives. In biblical Aramaic (the language of the Aramaic portions of Daniel and Ezra), דְּנָה serves as both a pronoun and a demonstrative adjective, equivalent to the Hebrew זֶה or זָאת, used to designate what is visible or immediately present.
H1836.emploi: This word appears 53 times in the Aramaic portions of the Old Testament, almost exclusively in the books of Ezra and Daniel. In Ezra (the books of the returns and the reconstruction of the Temple), it introduces letters, reports, and royal decrees: "here is the copy" (Ezra 4:11), "thus conceived" (Ezra 5:7). In Daniel, it accompanies the visions and dreams of the prophet: "your dream and the visions" (Daniel 2:28), "this writing" (Daniel 5:24). Its use remains consistent: it always designates something concrete, visible, or just mentioned, never something abstract or distant.
H1836.portee: This small word reminds us that biblical revelation speaks of real and verifiable facts: royal letters exist, the dream was truly seen, the writing was truly traced. It teaches the reader to pay attention to the concrete details of divine history, without getting trapped in speculation. It is a call to clarity and reality.

sens: City in the mountain of Judah
H1837.detail: 1. Danna is a small locality located in the mountainous region of southern Judah, probably to the south or southwest of Hebron. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:49, where it appears in the list of cities in the territory assigned to the tribe of Judah. The text specifies that it is also called Kirjath-Sanna and corresponds to the city of Debir, known as an important center in the mountain of Judah.
H1837.origine: The Hebrew name Danna literally means "you have judged" or "judgment." It likely derives from a root related to the idea of judgment or distinction, although the exact meaning of the name in the context of this city remains uncertain. Like many names of ancient cities, its etymology reflects either a significant action or a characteristic of the place.
H1837.emploi: Danna appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:49, where it is listed among the cities of Judah. This list establishes the territory that God assigned to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan. The identification of Danna with Kirjath-Sanna ("city of Sanna") and with Debir shows that this site bore several names at different times or according to different local traditions. Debir was an important city, the seat of a Canaanite king defeated by the Israelites.

sens: Capital of King Bela of Edom
H1838.detail: Dinhaba is the royal city of Bela, son of Beor, who ruled over Edom in ancient times. It is mentioned twice in the Bible, in the genealogy of the kings of Edom established before the monarchy of Israel. It is where this Edomite king established his seat of power.
H1838.origine: The name Dinhaba literally means "gives judgment" in Hebrew. It is formed from the root דִין (din = judgment, trial) and הבה (habah = gives), suggesting a city where royal justice reigns. This name reflects the king's function: to render justice to his people.
H1838.emploi: Dinhaba appears exactly twice in the Old Testament, both times in royal genealogies: in Genesis 36:32 and in 1 Chronicles 1:43. These two passages echo each other to enumerate the kings of Edom before the monarchy of Israel. Dinhaba is always designated as the city where Bela established his capital. Beyond these two mentions, Dinhaba disappears from biblical history, highlighting the antiquity of this Edomite reign.

sens: Descendants of Dan, son of Jacob
Members of the tribe of Israel descended from Dan
Inhabitants of the territory assigned to the tribe of Dan
H1839.detail: 1. The Danites are the direct descendants of Dan, one of the twelve sons of Jacob and founder of the tribe that bears his name (Judges 18:1). 2. This term designates the members of the tribe of Israel constituted by these descendants, who formed one of the twelve tribes of the chosen people and possessed their own territory (Judges 18:1: "the tribe of the Danites was seeking a possession"). 3. More broadly, the word applies to all the inhabitants of the territory allocated to this tribe, whether they are warriors, priests, or civilians (1 Chronicles 12:35: "Of the Danites, armed for war, twenty-eight thousand six hundred").
H1839.origine: The word "Danites" comes directly from the name "Dan" (דָּן), which means "judge" in Hebrew. Dan was the son of Jacob and Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant. The name of the tribe retains this etymology, and the term "Danites" (דָּנִי) is simply the adjective or demonym that designates those who belong to the family or tribe of Dan.
H1839.emploi: The term "Danites" appears five times in the provided usages, primarily in the book of Judges and once in Chronicles. It describes the members of this tribe at key moments in their history: during the calling of Samson (Judges 13:2, where Manoah is presented as a Danite), during the migration of the tribe in search of territory (Judges 18:1 and 18:11), during the establishment of an illegal cult (Judges 18:30), and during the counting of warriors in the time of David (1 Chronicles 12:35). The context shows a tribe that plays an important role in the history of Israel, but also a tribe often involved in troubling episodes or on the fringes of God's will.
H1839.portee: The Danites remind the reader that each tribe of Israel had its place in God's plan, but also that belonging to the chosen people was not a guarantee of faithfulness. Their history, particularly their migrations and religious compromises, shows how a community can stray from God's ways while remaining numerically strong and militarily capable. It is an invitation to examine whether our own belonging to the Church of Christ is accompanied by true obedience.

sens: A young Jew from the tribe of Judah, taken captive during the first exile to Babylon
A man gifted with the divine ability to interpret dreams and visions
A counselor and minister to King Nebuchadnezzar, and later to the kings of Persia
A prophet who receives visions concerning the end times
A man noted for his piety and faithfulness to God despite the exile
H1840G.detail:
1. Daniel is primarily a young man from the royal house of Judah, a young boy when the Babylonians deport him (Daniel 1:6) and put him in service to their king. He initially bears his Hebrew name, meaning "God is my judge."

2. God grants him an extraordinary gift: he can interpret dreams and visions, making him indispensable to King Nebuchadnezzar. Daniel 1:17 reports that "God gave these four young men knowledge and skill in all literature and wisdom; and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams."

3. Thanks to this gift, he becomes one of the highest advisors to the Babylonian king and retains his influence through the reigns of successive kings, until the rise of the Persian empire.

4. Starting in the third year of King Belshazzar's reign, Daniel himself receives spectacular visions about the future of the world and the coming kingdoms (Daniel 8:1).

5. The prophet Ezekiel cites him as a man of exemplary piety, and throughout his exile in Babylon, Daniel maintains his faithfulness to God despite the temptations and pressures of the pagan court.
H1840G.origine: The name Daniel means "God is my judge" (from the Hebrew "el" = God, and "din" = to judge). This name reflects the belief that only God truly judges and administers justice. The book of Daniel, written at the end of the Babylonian exile, bears his name because it recounts his prophetic visions and experiences of exile. This name fits within the tradition of theophoric names (containing the name of God) that reflect Israel's faith.
H1840G.emploi: Daniel is mentioned 23 times in the Hebrew Bible. The prophet Ezekiel cites him in chapter 14 among the righteous. The book of Daniel recounts his entire life: his childhood in captivity, his training at the Babylonian court (Daniel 1), his interpretations of dreams that elevate him to high responsibilities, and his personal visions in chapters 7 to 12. The king gives him a Babylonian name, Belteshazzar, to identify him in Babylon, but his faithfulness to his faith never wavers. From Daniel 8 onward, Daniel himself becomes the visionary who receives prophetic revelations from God about the future until the end of time.
H1840G.portee: Daniel shows every believer in spiritual or temporal exile that one can remain faithful to God and His principles even in the midst of a hostile culture. His personal integrity and quiet courage in the face of pagan challenges inspire those who seek to honor God in a secular world. His prophetic visions encourage the oppressed to believe that God is in control of history and that His plan is being fulfilled despite human empires.

sens: son of David and Abigail
second son of David born in Hebron
H1840H.detail: 1. Daniel is the second son of David, born of his marriage to Abigail of Carmel. His name means "God is my judge." He appears in the list of David's children mentioned in 1 Chronicles 3:1, where he is clearly identified as "the second" after Amnon.
H1840H.origine: The name Daniel comes from Hebrew and literally means "God is my judge": it combines "El" (God) and "din" (to judge). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, which was common in Israelite families to express trust in the Lord. The text in Chronicles also notes that he was called Chileab, another name given to the same child.
H1840H.emploi: Daniel, son of David, is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:1, where the list of David's sons born in Hebron is presented. This unique mention shows that unlike his brothers Amnon, Absalom, Adonijah, and Solomon, Daniel did not play any notable political or religious role in Israel's history. He remains a minor figure in the Davidic royal genealogy.
H1840H.portee: This Daniel illustrates a often forgotten reality: many biblical characters, even those from the royal family, remain in the shadows of history. His existence reminds us that God sees all His children, both great and small, and that the significance of a life is not measured solely by what is written about it.

sens: Man from the priestly tribe of Ithamar, returned from exile
Signer of the covenant under Nehemiah
H1841G.detail:
1. Daniel is a priest, son of the family of Ithamar, mentioned upon the return from exile in Babylon. He appears in the list of family leaders who return to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:2).
2. This same Daniel (or a namesake from the same period) is among the signers of the covenant that the people make under Nehemiah to observe the Law of God (Nehemiah 10:6). He represents the priests committed to restoring worship and faithfulness to the Lord.
H1841G.origine: The name Daniel means "God is my judge" in Hebrew. It is a theophoric name, where the term "El" (God) affirms that only God judges justly. This name was borne by several individuals in the Bible. This one, active at the time of the return from exile (around 458 B.C. according to the account of Ezra), belongs to the priestly lineage of Ithamar, brother of Eleazar.
H1841G.emploi: Daniel is mentioned twice in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, both dated to the time of the return from exile after the Babylonian captivity. In Ezra 8:2, he is listed among the priestly family leaders who return with Ezra. In Nehemiah 10:6, he seals the covenant of the people, testifying to the commitment of the priests to uphold the Law. This Daniel is not the famous prophet of the book of Daniel, but a contemporary of the return, representing the restored ecclesiastical order.

sens: A prophet from the time of the exile in Babylon
A young man deported from Judah and raised in the king's court
A man renowned for interpreting dreams and riddles
A minister of the king of Babylon, then of the Persian empire
A man of great moral purity and unwavering faithfulness to God
H1841H.detail:
1. Daniel is a prophet mentioned during the Babylonian exile: the prophet Ezekiel refers to him as a righteous man, alongside Noah and Job (Ezekiel 14:14). He is an emblematic figure of holiness.

2. Daniel was deported to Babylon during the first conquest of Jerusalem; the king gave him the Babylonian name Belteshazzar (Daniel 1:7). He grew up in the royal court, trained to serve the king.

3. His remarkable gift is interpreting dreams and riddles: the king specifically requests him to explain his enigmatic dreams that no one else can solve (Daniel 2:27; 5:12). This ability comes from God.

4. Daniel becomes a powerful minister of the king of Babylon, then of the Persian empire: he is elevated to the second position in the kingdom (Daniel 2:48-49) and retains his influence even after the fall of Babylon (Daniel 6:2-3).

5. He is noted for his uncompromising piety and faithfulness to God despite dangers: he refuses idolatry, prays despite the royal prohibition, and God miraculously protects him in the lion's den (Daniel 6:5-28).
H1841H.origine: The name Daniel literally means "God is my judge" in Hebrew: it expresses that God alone judges actions and hearts. This young Jew bears a name that summarizes his deep conviction: his faithfulness to God despite the pressure of a pagan regime. The Hebrew/Aramaic name דָּנִיֵּאל has produced the Hebrew form in the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) and has been preserved in Jewish and Christian tradition.
H1841H.emploi: Daniel is named 46 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the book that bears his name and a mention by the prophet Ezekiel. The book of Daniel covers his entire life in Babylon: his deportation and training at court (chapter 1), his interpretations of dreams (chapters 2 and 4-5), his trial in the lion's den (chapter 6), and his own prophetic visions about future empires (chapters 7-12). Through these accounts, Daniel is presented as a man who maintains his purity and faithfulness to God in the heart of an idolatrous empire while becoming an influential advisor to successive kings. His prophecies concerning the end times occupy a central place in biblical eschatology.
H1841H.portee: Daniel models what it means to remain faithful to God in a hostile and secular environment: he never compromises his faith, even when it puts him in danger. His story teaches that God exalts those who sincerely seek Him and refuse idolatry, and that He protects His faithful servants. His prophecies, particularly those of the 70 weeks (Daniel 9), are at the heart of the Christian understanding of the end times and the announcement of the Messiah.

sens: locality in Palestine mentioned during the census of King David
H1842.detail: 1. Dan-Jaan is a locality or region in Palestine mentioned only once in the Bible, during the account of the census ordered by King David. The text of 2 Samuel 24:6 indicates that the king's commissioners sent agents there to count the people, while they were also going to Gilead and near Sidon. The name may refer to a place located near Dan, the northern city of Israel, or refer to a border area of the conquered territory.
H1842.origine: The name Dan-Jaan combines two elements: Dan, the name of an important city in northern Israel (associated with the tribe of Dan), and Jaan (or Yaân), whose exact meaning remains uncertain. According to some ancient traditions, Dan-Jaan could be another name for Ijon (Aïyôn in Hebrew), a locality in the northern region. The very existence and precise location of Dan-Jaan remain debated by historians, as the place appears only once in the preserved biblical texts.
H1842.emploi: Dan-Jaan appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 24:6, in the context of the great census ordered by David. This census, undertaken by Joab and his officers, covers all Israel and Judah. The passage lists several regions visited: Gilead, the land of Tachthim-Hodshi, and Dan-Jaan, before heading towards the vicinity of Sidon. The unique mention of this locality makes it difficult to ascertain its exact geographical situation or its role in the history of Israel.

sens: What one knows, what one has learned or understood
The opinion one forms about something
The judgment one makes
Wisdom, instruction
H1843.detail: 1. Knowledge is what a person possesses in their mind: what they know, have learned, or understood. It is the content of their knowledge. When God "knows," He knows everything perfectly (Job 37:16: "He whose knowledge is perfect"). 2. It is also the opinion one forms on a subject — what one thinks or believes to be true. Elihu wants to "expose his thought" (Job 32:10), that is, to say what he thinks, his personal judgment. 3. Judgment is the result of this reflection: the conclusion one draws about something. Elihu takes "his reasons from on high" (Job 36:3), he exposes the conclusions he has drawn. 4. Wisdom or instruction that comes from experience and learning: it is knowledge that enriches and guides the one who possesses it.
H1843.origine: The Hebrew word דֵּעַ (dea) comes from a root that means "to know," "to be acquainted with." It is a noun that designates the action and its result: the knowledge itself. In the Old Testament, this same root appears in other forms, always related to the idea of perceiving, understanding, or recognizing something through experience or intellect. When one "knows" someone, one recognizes them; when one "knows" a truth, one understands it.
H1843.emploi: This word appears five times in the book of Job, always in the speeches of Elihu (chapters 32 to 37), the young friend of Job who speaks after the three elders. Elihu presents himself as someone who has knowledge and wants to share it: he wants to make known his feeling (Job 32:6), expose his thought (Job 32:10), say what he thinks (Job 32:17). He takes his reasons from on high — he bases his conclusions on high principles (Job 36:3). Finally, he speaks of God whose knowledge is perfect (Job 37:16): a complete and flawless knowledge. The word thus expresses both limited and imperfect human knowledge and the divine knowledge that is absolute.
H1843.portee: Knowledge, in the Bible, is never merely theoretical: it is an understanding that should inspire action and the fear of God. Elihu reminds us that possessing knowledge also means having the right and duty to share it with others. But above all, seeing that God possesses perfect knowledge should humble us: in the face of God's infinite knowledge, our knowledge remains very limited, and this is a reason to trust Him rather than to be proud of what we know.

sens: What one knows, what one is familiar with — acquired through learning or experience
Understanding, discernment — the ability to judge and grasp the meaning of things
Feeling, opinion — what one thinks or feels within oneself
Practical wisdom, intelligence — the know-how that guides action
The knowledge of God — the fact of knowing and recognizing Him as God
H1844.detail:
1. What one knows, what one is familiar with: this is consciousness, information, what has been learned. In 1 Samuel 2:3, the Lord "knows" everything: He possesses total and infallible knowledge of all actions.
2. Understanding and discernment: the ability to grasp the meaning of something, to judge pertinently. In Jeremiah 3:15, the shepherds will feed the people "with intelligence and wisdom" — they guide with understanding.
3. Feeling, opinion: what one personally thinks or feels within oneself. In Job 36:4, Elihu assures that his words are true and his "feelings" sincere — what he believes and expresses about himself.
4. Practical wisdom, intelligence: knowledge that becomes action, applied judgment. In Isaiah 28:9, it is asked "to whom shall wisdom be taught" — knowledge that transforms.
5. The knowledge of God: recognizing who God is, knowing Him through His works and revelation. In Isaiah 11:9, "the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the Lord" — everyone will recognize and understand Him.
H1844.origine: The word de'ah comes from a root (yd') that means "to know, to be acquainted with." This root primarily evokes knowledge through experience or observation: it is to see something and retain it. In Hebrew, "to know" God never means merely to have information; it is to recognize Him, to experience Him, to respect Him. The word thus designates both raw knowledge and deep understanding, a clear awareness of a reality.
H1844.emploi: This word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in poetic and prophetic texts. It designates sometimes the universal knowledge of God (1 Samuel 2:3: the Lord knows everything), sometimes human knowledge in the sense of understanding (Jeremiah 3:15: shepherds full of intelligence), and sometimes intimate conviction, feeling (Job 36:4). In Isaiah 11:9 and 28:9, it takes on prophetic or sapiential hues: it is the knowledge of God that fills the earth, or the wisdom that must be taught. The word always conveys a note of certainty and relevance — one truly knows, one deeply understands.
H1844.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the knowledge of God is not an abstract theory, but a living reality. To know God according to the Bible is to recognize Him in His acts, to listen to Him, to obey Him. It is also to discover that God alone knows all things perfectly. This invites us to seek this heart knowledge that transforms life and understanding of the world.

sens: father of Eliasaph, prince of the tribe of Gad at the time of the census at Sinai
H1845.detail: Deuel is a man from the time of the Exodus and the wilderness, father of Eliasaph who was designated as chief of the tribe of Gad during the great census of the Israelites at Sinai (Numbers 1:14). His name appears each time Eliasaph fulfills his duties as prince: during the presentation of offerings for the dedication of the tabernacle (Numbers 7:42), and at the departure from the wilderness when Eliasaph led the army of Gad (Numbers 10:20). He is also called Reuel in the list of Numbers 2:14.
H1845.origine: The name Deuel means "they know God," formed from the Hebrew "de" ("they") and "uel" ("God"). This man bears a theophoric name (which contains the name of God), common in Israel, expressing a relationship with the divine. He is also known by the name Reuel in certain biblical contexts.
H1845.emploi: Deuel is mentioned four times in the Bible, all in the book of Numbers, and always as the father of Eliasaph. He appears in the account of the census of the tribes at Sinai (Numbers 1), in the description of the offerings of the princes for the dedication of the tabernacle (Numbers 7), and in the report of the departure from the wilderness (Numbers 10). Although Deuel is the father, it is his son Eliasaph who acts and occupies a central place as the spiritual and military leader of Gad. Deuel represents the generation of fathers who left Egypt with Moses.

sens: to go out (referring to a flame or light)
to dry up, to wither (referring to a spring or watercourse)
to disappear, to be annihilated
H1846.detail: 1. To go out is primarily the action of a light or flame that ceases to burn and darkens. Job 18:5-6 illustrates this well: "The lamp of the wicked will go out"; the lamp above him will go out — it is the image of a life that loses its brightness and sinks into darkness. 2. The word also describes a watercourse or spring that dries up and disappears: Job 6:17 speaks of waters that "dry up" under the heat of the sun, their bed becoming dry. 3. Figuratively, to extinguish means to be annihilated or to completely disappear: when the lamp of the wicked goes out (Proverbs 13:9), it is his fortune, his future, all his existence that are annihilated under God's judgment.
H1846.origine: The Hebrew verb דָּעַךְ comes from a root that evokes the idea of causing to cease, to disappear. In Hebrew, related words carry the image of the moment when a light ceases or when water flows away. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), this word is translated by terms meaning "to extinguish" or "to disappear." The central image is that of extinction: everything that burns or flows can be stopped, cease.
H1846.emploi: The verb דָּעַךְ appears about 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in poetic and wisdom literature (Job, Psalms, Proverbs). In Job, it describes the extinction of a light or the drying up of water — images of the ruin of the wicked. In Psalms 118:12, it shows how enemies like a fire of thorns quickly go out. In Proverbs, especially 13:9 and 20:20, it contrasts the joyful light of the righteous with the lamp of the wicked that goes out: this extinction is a consequence of divine judgment. The word thus carries a strong moral and eschatological hue: extinction is never neutral; it expresses the elimination of evil.
H1846.portee: This word reminds the reader that evil has no lasting future: like a flame without fuel, like a spring without water, it goes out. For the believer, it is a promise of comfort: the wicked, however powerful they may seem, will see their light disappear. It is also an invitation to watch over one's own moral life: on what lamp does my life depend? Will it shine or go out?

sens: What one knows, what one perceives through sight, hearing, or experience
Acquired skill, mastered technique
Understanding, judgment, the ability to discern right from wrong
Conscience, moral clarity or intention
Practical wisdom and prudence
H1847.detail:
1. Knowledge is primarily what one knows through experience or learning: to have knowledge of something means to have learned it, seen it, or perceived it. Thus, the tree of the "knowledge" of good and evil in Genesis 2:9 is the tree whose fruit would give the one who eats it an experiential understanding of good and evil.
2. Knowledge also refers to the skill and competence acquired through practice: Bezalel, filled with the Spirit, receives "skill" (Exodus 31:3) — it is a know-how, a technical mastery in the art of constructing the tabernacle.
3. It also encompasses discernment, the ability to understand and judge rightly. An intelligent man for whom "knowledge is easy" (Proverbs 14:6) possesses this faculty to quickly understand what escapes the scoffer.
4. Knowledge can also refer to conscience or clarity: "you will act without knowledge" (Deuteronomy 19:4) speaks of an action committed without intention, without awareness of wrongdoing.
5. Finally, it encompasses wise and practical wisdom: "apply your heart to my knowledge" (Proverbs 22:17) invites one to acquire not an abstract knowledge, but a discernment of life.
H1847.origine: The Hebrew word da'at (דַּעַת) comes from the root yada (ידע), which means "to know." This root primarily evokes knowledge through direct experience, through contact: that is why it can also mean "to have intimate relationships." The word thus designates less abstract or theoretical knowledge than lived knowledge, acquired through experience or learning. The root yada is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible and structures the entire biblical meaning of the relationship with God.
H1847.emploi: The word appears 90 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is concentrated in the wisdom books — particularly Proverbs, where it often returns to explore the paths of wisdom and the formation of judgment. It also appears regularly in Job (where the knowledge of God and divine mysteries are discussed), the Psalms, and Ecclesiastes. In the historical and prophetic books, it generally denotes competence, skill, or moral awareness. Translations vary according to context: "skill" when knowledge is systematic or taught, "knowledge" when it is more general, "understanding" when it emphasizes judgment and discernment.
H1847.portee: This word reminds us that knowledge, in the Bible, is never purely theoretical or abstract. To know is to have a lived experience, a transformation of the heart. True knowledge of God is not merely a matter of doctrine, but of a personal encounter that changes the way one lives. It is also a call to cultivate discernment within oneself, the practical wisdom that allows one to distinguish right from wrong and to act righteously.

sens: Malicious words that discredit someone
Lies or accusations made to dishonor
Harm to reputation through calumny
H1848.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the act of speaking against someone, addressing them with words aimed at dishonoring them. In Psalms 50:20, the psalmist reproaches the one who "slanders the son of his mother": it is sitting down and uttering malicious words against a brother, a person from one's own family. It is a discourse that wounds and destroys reputation.
2. More broadly, it encompasses any accusation or slander made to tarnish someone, whether true or false. The word evokes the image of someone opening their mouth to spit out poisoned words against another, ruining their honor and place in the community.
H1848.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that fundamentally means "to speak" or "to say," with the idea of a hostile word directed against. In biblical Hebrew, words from this family denote accusations or gossip. The primary meaning is that of a "fault" or a "defect" that one reproaches someone for, which naturally extends to slander and calumny.
H1848.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 50:20, in a context of moral reproach addressed to one who claims to serve God while slandering their neighbor. The psalmist enumerates the sins of the heart of the one who speaks against their brother — it is a grave sin in the eyes of God, as it violates the commandment to love one's neighbor and to preserve peace in the community of Israel.
H1848.portee: This word reminds us that slanderous words and unfounded accusations are a serious sin before God, even — or especially — if the one who utters them claims to be pious. The psalmist teaches us that one who delights in slandering their brother contradicts their worship and faith. It is a warning for the believer: to watch over their tongue and refuse to participate in rumors or calumnies is an act of faithfulness to God.

sens: To deliver violent blows to something or someone
To hit a door or surface to signal one's presence
To press hard, to accelerate or intensify an action
H1849.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to deliver violent or repeated physical blows: it is the brutal gesture of one who strikes to hurt or dominate. In Judges 19:22, the men "struck at the door" violently to force entry, demonstrating the aggressiveness of the action.
2. To strike at a door or on a surface to request entry or attract attention: this is a gentler use of the same gesture. In Song of Solomon 5:2, the beloved "knocks" at the door of his beloved for her to open, a tender yet insistent call.
3. To force or press someone to accelerate, intensify their effort: this is a figurative use where the verb means "to push hard." In Genesis 33:13, Jacob refuses to "force" the pace of his nursing sheep and cattle, for they would perish from exhaustion.
H1849.origine: The Hebrew verb dāphaq comes from a root that expresses the idea of a blow, a violent shock. It paints the image of one who strikes with force and intention. The word belongs to a family of Hebrew terms related to violent movements and physical impacts. In the Hebrew Bible, it describes both the act of striking to harm and the more neutral action of knocking at a door.
H1849.emploi: The verb dāphaq is rare in the Hebrew Bible: only three occurrences are known to us. It appears in very different contexts, demonstrating its versatility. In Genesis 33:13, it describes the act of forcing the pace; in Judges 19:22, it refers to blows struck at a door in a situation of aggression; in Song of Solomon 5:2, it is the call of the beloved who gently knocks. The context entirely changes the tone of the gesture: from violent to gentle, from destructive to inviting.
H1849.portee: This word reminds us that force can be used to do harm, but also to call tenderly: it all depends on the intention and context. For the believer, it invites one to seek discernment between violence that destroys and insistence that expresses love. In the Song, the knock of the beloved becomes an image of the desire for intimacy and communion; it speaks to us of God who "knocks" gently at the door of our hearts.

sens: Stage in the desert where the Israelites camped during the Exodus
H1850.detail: Dophka is a place mentioned in the account of the Israelites' journey through the desert after their departure from Egypt. It is a stop between the desert of Sin and Alush, where the people rested and set up camp (Numbers 33:12–13).
H1850.origine: The name Dophka comes from a Hebrew root evoking the idea of striking or hitting. It may refer to a distinctive geographical feature of the place, perhaps steep rocks or rugged terrain where the sound of footsteps or impacts could be heard. The primary meaning of the name suggests a physically distinctive location in the Sinai desert.
H1850.emploi: Dophka appears only twice in the Bible, both in chapter 33 of Numbers, which enumerates the forty-two stops of the Israelites' journey through the desert. It is a geographical list without dramatic narrative, intended to document the exact path taken by God's people over forty years. Dophka is among the first stops after the departure from Egypt, between the desert of Sin and Alush.

sens: Who has little flesh, who is very thin
Of small size or little thickness
Who is fine, light, almost imperceptible
H1851.detail:
1. Maigre first refers to a physical creature that lacks flesh: the lean cows in Pharaoh's dream devoured the fat ones, symbolizing famine (Genesis 41:3). This evokes extreme thinness, emaciation.
2. Maigre also refers to what is small, fine, almost nothing: the manna was like something tiny, thin, resembling frost flakes (Exodus 16:14). The image emphasizes smallness and fineness.
3. Finally, maigre refers to what is tenuous, light, barely perceptible: the voice of the Lord after the earthquake was a gentle and light whisper (1 Kings 19:12). It is the absence of apparent power, but a delicate presence.
H1851.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of fineness, of thinness. It first designates what is reduced to fine powder or what diminishes. The root daq- is used in several contexts to express the absence of thickness or substance: fine, small, tenuous things.
H1851.emploi: This word appears thirteen times in the Old Testament, especially in the narratives of Genesis (the dream of Pharaoh about the lean cows and the lean ears: six times) and in legal or visionary texts. It describes hungry and weak cows (Genesis 41), sterile ears burned by the wind (Genesis 41), the fine dust of the desert (Exodus 16:14), and even the light voice of God (1 Kings 19:12). The word can also qualify a bodily defect (a lean ulcer in Leviticus 13:30) or incense reduced to fine powder (Leviticus 16:12). Its meaning varies from extremely thin to simply fine and almost imperceptible.
H1851.portee: This word teaches that hunger and deprivation are realities that God knows: Pharaoh's dream reminds us that God warns of impending famines. It also shows that God manifests not through noise or visible power, but in delicacy, in a light whisper. For the believer, this invites us to seek God not in the spectacular, but in discretion and tenderness.

sens: Fine and light fabric that is spread out
What covers and envelops like a veil
H1852.detail:
1. The word designates a fine and light fabric, shaped as such — not a thick garment or a rigid object. In Isaiah 40:22, God "stretches out the heavens like a light fabric": the image is that of a supple material that is unfolded and stretched, like one would spread a piece of cloth above oneself. It is not a solid or heavy construction, but something delicately arranged.
2. By extension, the word evokes what envelops, covers, and creates a visible separation or boundary — a kind of veil or curtain. The fabric is what is seen, which delineates a space, which can be extended or folded. In the same passage, the image becomes that of a tent: the heavens are like a fabric that is unfolded to create a dwelling, that is, to shelter and define a habitable space.
H1852.origine: The Hebrew word דֹּק (doq) refers to the idea of something fine, subtle, that can be stretched and unfolded. The root suggests a light material, rather than a thick or massive substance. It is a concrete term: it evokes the action of stretching a fabric, the visual and tactile image of a fabric being manipulated.
H1852.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 40:22. This unique passage is a cosmic vision: the prophet contemplates God sitting above the circle of the earth and sees the celestial expanse not as a rigid vault — as it was imagined in antiquity — but as a fine and light fabric, unfolded like a tent. This rare image accentuates the lightness and flexibility of creation: the heavens, however vast and impressive they may seem, are merely a veil between the majesty of God and the world He inhabits.
H1852.portee: This image invites us to see creation from a new angle: not as an immutable and terrible construction, but as something subtle and beautiful, stretched by God for our dwelling. It reminds us that even what seems infinite and eternal — the starry heavens — remains light and dependent on the Creator. This can fill us with confidence: if God stretches out the heavens like a simple fabric, we too can rest in His providence.

sens: Son of Joktan, antediluvian Arab patriarch
Territory or Arab people
H1853.detail:
1. Dikla is a man from the time of the Patriarchs, one of the twelve sons of Joktan listed in Genesis 10:27 and 1 Chronicles 1:21. He appears in the genealogy of the Semitic peoples who settled in Arabia after the dispersion of Babel.
2. The name also seems to designate an ancient Arab territory or tribe, probably a fertile region known for its date palms, although the Bible does not provide precise geographical details about this people.
H1853.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "grove of palms" or "palm grove." It reflects the importance of palms in the economy and landscape of ancient Arabia. This proper name, like those of his brothers (Jerah, Hazarmaveth, Ophir, Sheba), evokes both a person and the region they populated or governed.
H1853.emploi: Dikla appears twice in the Bible, in the genealogy of the sons of Joktan: in Genesis 10:27 and in 1 Chronicles 1:21, which repeat exactly the same passage. These two occurrences form the list of Arab peoples descended from Joktan. Dikla is situated there between Uzal and Hadoram among the brothers. The context suggests that it is a tribe or region of Arabia, possibly identifiable with a historically productive area.

sens: Reduce something to powder or dust by crushing
Grind, pulverize grains or food
Completely destroy, annihilate
Be reduced to powder (passive form)
H1854.detail:
1. Reduce something to powder or dust by crushing: it literally means to pulverize a solid material until it is transformed into fine powder. Josiah does this with the altars and idols he destroys: he reduces them to dust and throws away the remnants (2 Chronicles 34:7).

2. Grind, pulverize grains or food: grinding grain to make flour, or reducing it to fine particles. The prophet Isaiah speaks of a people who will crush mountains like one crushes grain (Isaiah 41:15).

3. Completely destroy, annihilate: render something completely unusable and worthless. Moses burns the golden calf and grinds it to reduce this symbol of rebellion to powder which he throws into a torrent (Deuteronomy 9:21).

4. Be reduced to powder (passive form): undergo the action of being crushed and pulverized. This usage describes the resulting state of being crushed.
H1854.origine: The Hebrew verb daqaq expresses the action of reducing to very fine particles. Its root evokes the sound and action of breaking: it is related to the word for "fine," "delicate," emphasizing how something becomes formless and reduced to powder. The word appears in contexts of ritual or military destruction, always with the idea of total and irreversible reduction.
H1854.emploi: This verb appears 12 times in the Old Testament, concentrated in the historical books and the prophets. It often describes the action of destroying idols and altars: Josiah reduces them to dust (2 Chronicles 15:16; 34:7), King Asa does the same with the idol of Ashtoreth (2 Chronicles 15:16). Moses uses it to annihilate the golden calf after burning it (Deuteronomy 9:21; Exodus 32:20). In prophetic texts, the word takes on a broader significance: Isaiah and Micah use it to describe how God will crush enemies and obstacles, even turning mountains to dust (Isaiah 41:15; Micah 4:13). In all cases, the word emphasizes the intensity of destruction — not just breaking, but reducing to nothing.
H1854.portee: This word reminds every reader that God definitively destroys all that opposes Him — idols, altars of evil, spiritual obstacles. It also shows how God shatters rebellion and pride: nothing can withstand His power. For the believer, it is an assurance that sin and all that represents it are destined for destruction, and an invitation to place trust only in God.

sens: To break into pieces, reduce to fragments
To crush, completely smash
Figuratively: to annihilate, destroy a power or a kingdom
H1855.detail:
1. To break something into pieces: this is the concrete and physical sense. When the stone in Nebuchadnezzar's dream strikes the statue, it "breaks" its feet of iron and clay (Daniel 2:34), reducing them to fragments. The lions "break" the bones of Daniel's accusers (Daniel 6:24): this is the complete destruction of a body.
2. To crush to annihilation: this sense pushes the idea of fragmentation further. The iron "breaks and crushes everything" (Daniel 2:40), suggesting an action of total and overwhelming destruction, leaving nothing standing.
3. To destroy a power or a reign: the word takes on a political and religious significance. The God of heaven "will break" all earthly kingdoms (Daniel 2:44), and the mysterious stone "has broken" the empire represented by the statue (Daniel 2:45). This is God's definitive victory over the powers of the world.
H1855.origine: The Aramaic verb דְּקַק (deqaq) comes from a root that expresses the idea of fragmenting, reducing to small pieces. In biblical Aramaic, this word is used primarily in the prophetic passages of the book of Daniel, where it describes both the physical and symbolic action of destruction. The same root exists in Hebrew with a comparable meaning: to shatter, to break.
H1855.emploi: The verb דְּקַק (deqaq) appears 9 times in the New Testament in biblical Aramaic, exclusively in the book of Daniel, chapters 2 and 6-7. It is central to the interpretation of the dream of the statue (Daniel 2), where it first describes the action of the supernatural stone that strikes and breaks the statue (verses 34-35, 45), then the action of iron that "breaks everything" (verse 40). The same verb reappears in chapter 6, where it describes the brutal action of the lions on Daniel's accusers. Finally, in Daniel 7, it characterizes the fourth beast that "breaks" and destroys (verses 7, 19, 23). The word always oscillates between the concrete (physical destruction) and the symbolic (annihilation of a political or divine power).
H1855.portee: This word reminds the reader that God controls history and breaks the human powers that oppose His kingdom. It invites trust: even the strongest empires, compared to iron, will be brought to nothing before the stone of God's eternal kingdom. For the Christian, it is a promise: obstacles, even massive ones, do not escape God's control.

sens: To pass through something or someone with a sharp weapon, create an opening
To strike fatally with a blade
To be pierced, to suffer a penetrating wound
To injure, to bruise
H1856.detail:
1. To pierce means to thrust a sharp weapon through a material or body: the result is a wound that goes all the way through. Phinehas "pierced" the two lovers of sin by running them through with one blow (Numbers 25:8), and Saul asks his armor-bearer to "pierce" him with the sword rather than fall alive into the hands of the enemy (1 Samuel 31:4).
2. The word designates the act of killing by means of a piercing weapon: the young man "pierced" the chief of the Shechemites, meaning he killed him by striking him with his weapon (Judges 9:54).
3. In the passive voice (to be pierced), the word describes the condition of one who has received a fatal wound: during the siege of Babylon, the "wounded" soldiers are those who have been pierced and lie powerless (Jeremiah 37:10).
4. In the context of divine judgment, to be pierced means to suffer a serious injury, a wound inflicted by God or His instruments: all those found will be "pierced" by the sword in the judgment of Isaiah 13:15.
H1856.origine: The Hebrew root דָּקַר (daqar) expresses the action of piercing, of transfixing, using a point or a sharp weapon. It evokes the image of a sharp and direct penetration. The word belongs to a small family of terms that share this idea of perforation or injury in the Old Testament.
H1856.emploi: The verb דָּקַר (daqar) appears about ten times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, Judges, Numbers) and prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zechariah, Lamentations). It describes acts of war and execution: the murder of enemies or criminals by a sharp weapon. It can take the broad meaning of "mortally wound" (1 Samuel 31:4, Judges 9:54) or describe the state of one who has been pierced (Jeremiah 37:10: "wounded"). In the context of divine judgment (Isaiah 13:15, Zechariah 12:10), it expresses a decisive and final injury. The variety of forms (active, passive) shows that the emphasis is sometimes on the agent who pierces, sometimes on the victim who suffers the wound.
H1856.portee: This word reminds us of the brutal reality of sin, war, and divine judgment in biblical history. When Zechariah speaks of the One who has been "pierced" (Zechariah 12:10), the early Christians recognized a prophecy of Christ's Passion. For the reader, to pierce remains the image of a deep injury, an irreparable rupture — whether it is sin that pierces life, or divine judgment that strikes at the heart.

sens: White and shiny substance that forms the interior of certain shells
Luxurious and beautiful object or material, used for decoration
H1858.detail:
1. Mother-of-pearl is the pearly, white, and lustrous substance that lines the interior of mollusk shells — it is what gives luster to pearls. In Esther 1:6, mother-of-pearl is featured on the floor of King Ahasuerus's palace, among the most precious materials: it contrasts with porphyry, marble, and black stones, creating a pavement of unparalleled richness and splendor.
2. By extension, mother-of-pearl refers to any decorative object made from this luxurious material, a symbol of refined beauty and wealth. Its unique use in Esther 1:6 shows that it only appears in the Bible to describe royal magnificence, never in an ordinary context.
H1858.origine: The Hebrew word דַּר (dar) literally means "mother-of-pearl" or "nacre." It is a rare term in biblical Hebrew, borrowed or related to exotic materials known primarily through trade and contacts with Eastern civilizations. Its unique occurrence in Esther 1:6 underscores its specialized character, designating a luxury reserved for royal courts.
H1858.emploi: The word דַּר (dar) appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Esther 1:6, in the grand description of Ahasuerus's palace. It is part of a list of the most precious and prestigious materials that the king could gather to build and decorate his residence: gold, silver, porphyry, marble, fine linen, and purple. Mother-of-pearl, included in this prestigious list, represents a natural luster and beauty that only the most powerful kings could afford to possess and display.
H1858.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not judge wealth in itself, but always places it in a human context: the magnificence of King Ahasuerus, displayed to impress and dominate, will lead to the humiliation of a queen and a crisis of power. Mother-of-pearl shines on the pavement, but it does not save the king from his own follies. For the Christian, it is an invitation not to confuse outward splendor with true greatness.

sens: period of time corresponding to the life of a human generation
group of people born at the same time
continuous succession of time from one era to another
H1859.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a human generation, that is, the group of people who live around the same time. It is the span of time it takes for one generation to be replaced by the next. In Daniel 4:3, when it is said that God's dominion "endures from generation to generation," it imagines the succession of groups of people who pass on the testimony of divine power.

2. The word also denotes the continuity of time that flows from one era to another. In Daniel 4:34, Nebuchadnezzar proclaims that God's reign persists "from generation to generation," meaning that His kingship transcends all ages, uninterrupted, from the past to the future, from the beginning to the end of time.
H1859.origine: The Aramaic word דָּר comes from the same root as the Hebrew דּוֹר (dor), which literally means "generation." The root evokes the idea of "dwelling" or "duration": a generation is the time during which a human community "dwells" or "inhabits" the earth. This word appears especially in passages where Scripture speaks of the divine permanence that persists through the changes of human generations.
H1859.emploi: The Aramaic word דָּר appears twice in the book of Daniel, in chapters 4:3 and 4:34, both in the context of the dream and interpretation received by King Nebuchadnezzar. In these two passages, the word is used to express the idea that the dominion and kingship of the God of Israel are eternal and unshakeable: they endure "from generation to generation," that is, through all changes and all periods of human history. The use of the word emphasizes the contrast between the fragility of human reigns and the permanence of God's kingdom.
H1859.portee: This word reminds the believer that, while human powers and empires pass away, God's authority remains firm from generation to generation. It highlights God's faithfulness through the centuries and encourages us to place our trust in Him rather than in earthly powers. It also invites us to live our generation with the awareness of being part of an unbroken chain of witnesses to God's greatness.

sens: Intense repulsion, deep disgust towards something abominable
Feeling of aversion and rejection towards what offends or revolts
State of ignominy, extreme dishonor
H1860.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes a visceral reaction of aversion and rejection: a deep disgust in the face of what is abominable. In Isaiah 66:24, the corpses of the rebels become an object of horror for all — a vision so revolting that it inspires disgust and distance. 2. It also refers to the feeling of moral and spiritual repulsion: that which is repugnant because it offends, because it is contrary to the just order. 3. Finally, the word takes on the meaning of opprobrium or lasting shame: in Daniel 12:2, the wicked will rise to eternal shame — not only ashamed, but objects of shame, despised forever.
H1860.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses aversion and rejection. Its image is that of repugnance towards what is abject or degrading. The word belongs to the family of terms of abjection and contempt in biblical Hebrew, where physical disgust and moral disgust are often intertwined.
H1860.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible. In Isaiah 66:24, it qualifies the effect that the corpses of the rebels have on those who see them — an inevitable spectacle of horror beyond present life. In Daniel 12:2, it describes the fate of the wicked at the resurrection: the eternal shame that will cover them forever, marking their definitive separation from the righteous. Both uses emphasize the ultimate rejection and repulsion that acts of rebellion entail.
H1860.portee: This word reminds the believer that rebellion against God carries irreversible and visible consequences: not only annihilation or condemnation, but opprobrium and contempt that all will recognize. It invites us to take seriously the gravity of apostasy and to fear the aversion that God turns away from those He saves.

sens: Pointed stick used to prod draft animals to move forward
Instrument of punishment or torture
Figuratively, that which prompts or stimulates the conscience
H1861A.detail: 1. The goad is a stick or rod with a sharp point, used by the driver of a team to prod oxen or donkeys to encourage them to move or obey. In 1 Samuel 13:21, it is mentioned alongside the agricultural tools that the Philistines sharpened: it could be straightened when its point became dull. 2. By extension, the goad can be used as an instrument of pain or punishment, striking the one who endures it. 3. In a metaphorical sense, in the New Testament, the goad represents anything that pricks or stimulates the conscience: a voice that awakens, a rebuke that prompts a reaction, or even the conviction that the Holy Spirit brings to the heart of the sinner.
H1861A.origine: The Hebrew word דַּרְבוֹן comes from a root that evokes the action of prodding or striking. It is a simple and concrete term, designating a tool of everyday agricultural and pastoral life in the ancient Near East. The word also appears in the form דָּרְבֹנָה (darbonah), an older or regional variant of the same instrument. In New Testament Greek, the corresponding word is κέντρον (kentron), literally "sting" or "point."
H1861A.emploi: The word appears only once in the provided biblical text, in 1 Samuel 13:21, in a context of Philistine domination. The Philistines, who monopolized ironwork, also controlled the maintenance of agricultural tools, including goads. This passage shows that the goad was an ordinary but essential tool of Israeli rural life, used daily to guide livestock. Its role in New Testament uses (notably in Acts 26:14, "It is hard for you to kick against the goads") makes it an image of resistance to divine will.
H1861A.portee: The goad reminds the reader that God uses various means to direct and correct us: circumstances, words, or even suffering. Understanding this word in its primary sense helps to grasp why the Bible chooses it to describe the voice that pricks the conscience. It is an invitation not to flee from this divine "sting," but to recognize it as a sign of love.

sens: Pointed rod used to prod and direct a draft animal
Figuratively: that which stimulates, that which prompts action
H1861B.detail:
1. The goad is a long pointed rod, often made of wood with a metal tip, that the plowman uses to prod oxen or donkeys and direct them in field work. It is a practical and common instrument in ancient agriculture (Ecclesiastes 12:13).
2. Figuratively, the goad refers to that which stimulates the mind or conscience, prompting reflection and progress. In Ecclesiastes 12:13, the words of the wise are compared to goads: they prick the reader's understanding just as a goad makes livestock move forward, prompting them to question and change direction.
H1861B.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of prodding or striking. The goad is the instrument that makes things move, that provokes a reaction. The image is very concrete: just as one prods an animal with a goad to make it advance, one pricks the soul with a word that awakens the conscience.
H1861B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ecclesiastes 12:13, where the author compares the words of the wise to goads. This comparison emphasizes the lively and stimulating force of wisdom: it does not leave one indifferent, it pricks, it makes one reflect, it pushes to action and obedience.
H1861B.portee: This word reminds us that the word of God and biblical wisdom are not dead or passive: they are alive, active, they touch our hearts and push us to change. Just as a goad awakens a sleeping animal, the right word awakens our conscience and sets us in motion towards what is good.

sens: Son of Mahol, one of the four most renowned wise men during the time of the united monarchy
Wise man surpassed in wisdom only by Solomon
H1862.detail:
