1. Darda is a man who lived during the time of the united monarchy in Israel. He is the son of Mahol and the brother of Ethan, Heman, and Calcol. All four were famous for their extraordinary wisdom: the Bible states that they enjoyed great renown among the neighboring nations (1 Kings 4:31).
2. Although Darda was one of the greatest wise men of his time, Solomon surpassed him in wisdom. The text of 1 Kings 4:31 specifically mentions him to demonstrate the superiority of King Solomon's wisdom: no other man, not even Darda with his three brothers, could match the wisdom that God had given to Solomon.
H1862.origine: The name Darda literally means "pearl of knowledge" (dar = pearl, da = knowledge). His father Mahol appears in the Bible only as the father of these four wise sons. No other details about their origins or deeds are provided.
H1862.emploi: Darda is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:31. He is listed among the four wisest men of Solomon's time: Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Calcol, and Darda, son of Mahol. The Bible cites them only to establish a contrast with Solomon's superhuman wisdom, which surpassed them all. These four wise men represent human excellence in wisdom, but even this excellence is eclipsed by the divine gift that Solomon received.
H1862.portee: The mention of Darda reminds the reader that ordinary wisdom, even the greatest and most renowned, remains human and limited. Only the wisdom that God gives — the one that Solomon asked for and received — transcends natural abilities. For the believer, this account invites the pursuit of wisdom that is not purely natural or intellectual, but the wisdom that comes from God.

sens: thorny plant that grows spontaneously in abandoned land
wild vegetation that invades places
symbol of curse and desolation
H1863.detail:
1. The bramble is a thorn-covered plant that grows naturally in uncultivated fields. In Genesis 3:18, after Adam's fall, God announces that the earth will produce thorns and brambles: this is a sign that work becomes burdensome and that creation suffers the consequences of sin.
2. When an area is abandoned or devastated, brambles invade the soil. Hosea 10:8 describes how thorns and brambles will grow on the destroyed altars of an idolatrous sanctuary: this is the image of a land given over to desolation, where the fruits of civilization disappear under wild vegetation.
3. The bramble becomes a biblical symbol of curse, ruin, and the absence of divine blessing. It represents what grows when order and organized life disappear, reminding us that sin and unfaithfulness produce destruction.
H1863.origine: The Hebrew word דַּרְדַּר (dardar) is a repeated or intensified formation derived from a root meaning to prick or pierce. This reduplicative structure (dar-dar) emphasizes the invasive and abundant nature of this harmful plant. The word directly reflects the rough and aggressive sound of the plant itself.
H1863.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, in contexts that emphasize the curse. In Genesis 3:18, at the heart of the fall narrative, the bramble is one of the first consequences of sin imprinted in creation. In Hosea 10:8, the bramble marks the ruin of the places of idolatrous worship: its appearance signals divine abandonment and the end of prosperity. In both cases, the bramble is never just a botanical plant, but a sign of the broken order of the world.
H1863.portee: For the believer, the bramble serves as a reminder that sin has concrete and visible consequences in the created world. It invites recognition that distancing from God produces ruin and chaos, but also hope that redemption will restore the order and blessing that God intended for His creation.

sens: cardinal direction of south, where the sun reaches its highest point
region or territory located to the south
south side of a building or space
H1864.detail:
1. The south is the direction of south, the point on the horizon where the sun reaches its highest. This is seen in Ecclesiastes 1:6 where the wind turns toward the south, then toward the north: it is an observation of the compass rose. It is also a region: in Deuteronomy 33:23, Naphtali "takes possession of the west and the south," which designates a geographical area.
2. The word often designates a side, a specific direction in a construction or space. In Ezekiel 40:27, a distance is measured "from one gate to another to the south," and in Ezekiel 40:44, a chamber has "its face to the south": this simply indicates the southern orientation of an entrance or room, as we would say "south facade" or "south wall."
H1864.origine: The Hebrew word is related to the idea of heat and brightness of the sun at its zenith. It literally designates "the warm, bright side" of the day. The root expresses the direction where the sun shines when its heat is most intense. It is a simple and concrete word, forged from the observation of the sky.
H1864.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the provided biblical texts, mainly in poetic books and prophetic descriptions. It is found in Ecclesiastes to describe the movements of the wind (1:6, 11:3), showing its meteorological usage. Ezekiel makes intensive use of it in his vision of the restored temple (chapters 40 to 42): he uses "south" as an architectural reference point to describe gates, chambers, and sides of spaces, always to specify a location. In Deuteronomy 33:23, it designates an inhabited region. The word is therefore directional (a cardinal point), geographical (a region), and architectural (a side, an orientation).
H1864.portee: Understanding that the south is just one direction among others helps the reader grasp how the Bible describes space and the orientation of the temple. It is an invitation to see how the sacred texts anchor the spiritual in the concrete and observable, using cardinal points and geography as means of clarity and precision. For those reading Ezekiel's visions, it is also a call to pay close attention to the architectural details, signs of the order and beauty of what will be built.

sens: That which flows freely, without hindrance
The state of one who is not a slave or captive
The absence of constraint or obligation
The right to return to one's property and family
The release of prisoners
A rest or remission granted by grace
H1865.detail:
1. In Exodus 30:23, the word refers to myrrh that "flows" of its own accord, not extracted by force: it is the best quality, that which naturally flows from the trunk. The image is one of unimpeded fluidity.

2. In Leviticus 25:10, during the jubilee, the "freedom" proclaimed in the land means that every Hebrew slave returns home to his family, his debts are canceled. It is an official and joyful liberation, inscribed in the law.

3. In Isaiah 61:1, the Lord anoints His servant to proclaim "freedom" to the captives: it is the release of prisoners, the return to the state of free and unenslaved persons.

4. In Jeremiah 34, King Zedekiah makes a pact to proclaim "freedom": he orders that every master release his Hebrew slave. This word refers to the legal act by which one grants freedom to a slave.

5. In Jeremiah 34:17, God turns the threat around: He proclaims against the treacherous people the "freedom" of the sword, pestilence, and famine. It is an ironic usage: the freedom given to plagues is their destructive free course.
H1865.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to flow" or "to stream": it primarily evokes that which flows naturally and without obstacle. By extension, it designates the state of one who runs freely, without hindrances. In Leviticus and Jeremiah, it applies to the institution of the liberation of Hebrew slaves: a cessation of obligation, a restored right.
H1865.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible. Once in Exodus 30:23 in a strictly concrete sense: the quality of myrrh. Six times in a legal and social sense: the freedom of the jubilee (Leviticus 25:10), the proclamation of the release of slaves (Jeremiah 34:8, 34:15, 34:17), the messianic deliverance of captives (Isaiah 61:1), and a mention in Ezekiel 46:17. The word thus enriches itself from the concrete (that which flows) to the legal and spiritual (the state of one who is freed).
H1865.portee: This word reminds the believer that true freedom is a gift from God, inscribed in His law and grace. In Isaiah 61:1, echoed by Jesus in Luke 4:18, it designates the spiritual liberation brought by the Messiah: the breaking of the chains of sin and judgment. For the Christian, it is a call not to remain enslaved, but to enter into the freedom that Christ has proclaimed and accomplished through His sacrifice.

sens: Small bird that flies quickly and builds its nest under roofs or overhangs
Image of lightness and swift flight
H1866.detail:
1. The swallow is a small bird known for its quick and graceful flight. It builds its nest from mud and straw, often under the eaves of houses or in sheltered places. It is a migratory bird that returns each spring. Psalm 84:4 shows the swallow finding a cozy nest near God's altars, symbolizing a safe refuge and a cherished home.
2. The swallow is also the biblical image of swift and light escape. Its lively and unpredictable movements make it a symbol of that which easily slips away. In Proverbs 26:2, a curse is compared to a swallow that flies away: just as one cannot hold a bird in flight, a baseless curse cannot settle on someone.
H1866.origine: The Hebrew word דְּרוֹר (déror) specifically designates the swallow. Its exact origin is uncertain, but it may be related to the idea of freedom or free flight, due to the swift and graceful movement of this bird. This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, always to evoke images of flight or refuge.
H1866.emploi: The word דְּרוֹר appears only twice in the Hebrew Scriptures, always in poetic books (Psalms and Proverbs). In each case, the swallow is used as an image: first as a bird that finds a peaceful refuge near the dwelling of God (Psalms 84:4), then as a symbol of that which escapes quickly and cannot be stopped (Proverbs 26:2). These two uses exploit the observable characteristics of the swallow — its rapid nesting and agile flight — to illustrate spiritual or moral realities.
H1866.portee: The swallow reminds us that even small creatures find their place and security with God. It also teaches us that a word or baseless curse has no hold: it disappears like a bird that flies away. It is an invitation not to fear vain accusations, and to seek our refuge in God.

sens: Name of a king of Persia mentioned in the Old Testament
H1867G.detail: Darius is the name of a Persian king. The only clear biblical usage is found in Nehemiah 12:22, where he is called "Darius the Persian." This most likely refers to Darius II, who ruled over the Persian empire from 424 to 404 B.C., during the years when Nehemiah governed Jerusalem after the Exile. It was under his authority that the Levites and priests were registered during the reconstruction of the Temple and Jerusalem.
H1867G.origine: The name "Darius" comes from Old Persian and means "he who possesses" or "master." It was the title held by several kings of the Persian Achaemenid dynasty, notably Darius I (the Great), founder of Persian power in the 6th century B.C., and his successors. In biblical Hebrew, it is written דָּֽרְיָ֫וֶשׁ (Daryavesh), which reproduces the Persian pronunciation.
H1867G.emploi: Darius is mentioned only once in the Bible: in Nehemiah 12:22. He is referred to as "Darius the Persian," under whose reign the heads of the Levites and priests were recorded during the religious reorganization of Jerusalem after the Exile. This historical mention occurs at the heart of the period when Nehemiah was restoring the city and its institutions. Although several kings bore the name Darius, the historical context (424-404 B.C.) identifies this one as Darius II.

sens: King of Persia who reigned after Cyrus
Monarch who allowed the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem
H1867H.detail:
1. Darius is the name of a Persian king who succeeded Cyrus and continued to reign over the Persian empire during the period of the return from exile. It was under his authority that the exiled Jews were able to continue their work (Ezra 4:5).
2. This king became famous in biblical history as the one under whose reign the prophets Haggai and Zechariah prophesied, during the reconstruction of the temple. The second year of his reign marked the renewal of prophetic activity in Judah (Haggai 1:1 and Zechariah 1:1).
H1867H.origine: The name Darius comes from Persian and means "lord" or "master." It was a royal title held by several kings of ancient Persia. The Bible mentions several sovereigns bearing this name: Darius the Mede, Darius son of Hystaspes (founder of the dynasty), and possibly others. The context of biblical usages indicates that it refers to the Darius whose reign coincided with the end of the Babylonian exile, likely Darius II according to scholars.
H1867H.emploi: Darius appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the books of Ezra, Haggai, and Zechariah, all concerning the period of the return from exile (circa 520 B.C.). He is mentioned to precisely date events: Ezra 4:5 places his reign after that of Cyrus; Haggai and Zechariah date their prophecies according to the years and months of Darius's reign, notably "the second year" (Haggai 1:1, Zechariah 1:1). These temporal references highlight his political importance as a guarantor of the stability that allowed for the reconstruction of the temple and the fulfillment of messianic prophecies.
H1867H.portee: Darius represents in the biblical narrative the divine providence that prepares favorable conditions for the return of the chosen people and the restoration of worship. His reign coincides with the prophetic renewal and shows that God acts even through foreign kings to accomplish His redemptive plan for His people.

sens: King who succeeded Belshazzar and ruled over the Babylonian kingdom
Sovereign during the time of the exile and the return of Israel
H1867I.detail:
1. Darius was a king who ruled after the fall of Belshazzar, the last king of Babylon. He succeeded to the throne of the Chaldean kingdom and became the master of Babylon (Daniel 9:1). According to tradition, he was the son of Ahasuerus and of Median descent, making him a ruler from the Medes.

2. He played an important role during the time of the return of the Israelites from exile. Darius was king at the time when the prophet Daniel received visions and messages from God. The angel Gabriel came to Daniel to help and support him from the very first year of Darius's reign (Daniel 11:1).
H1867I.origine: The name Darius (דָּֽרְיָ֫וֶשׁ in Hebrew) comes from Persian and means "lord" or "one who holds the law." It is a royal Persian name borne by several kings of Persia throughout history. The name appears in biblical texts to designate rulers from the time of the Babylonian exile.
H1867I.emploi: Darius is mentioned twice in the Bible, both in the book of Daniel. In Daniel 9:1, he is presented as the son of Ahasuerus who became king of the Chaldean kingdom after Belshazzar. In Daniel 11:1, he is called "Darius the Mede," and it is during his reign that God sends the angel Gabriel to strengthen and support Daniel in his visions. These two passages place Darius as a king contemporary with major events of the Judean exile and the beginning of the return.
H1867I.portee: Darius embodies the political authority of the world surrounding God's people in exile. Through him, the Bible shows that even under a foreign king, God's plans for Israel progress: angels intervene, Daniel's visions are fulfilled, and God controls history despite the apparent dominance of world powers.

sens: King of Persia who allowed the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem
Persian sovereign during the time of the exile and the return
H1868G.detail:
1. Darius is a Persian king mentioned in the book of Ezra as the one who authorized and supported the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. After ordering searches in the archives of Babylon to verify the ancient decrees (Ezra 6:1), he decided to personally finance the work and protect the project with a royal edict (Ezra 6:12). This is a crucial moment where divine will is fulfilled through the decision of a foreign monarch.
2. The name "Darius" means "lord" or "one who holds power." It is likely referring to Darius I, the founder of the Persian dynasty, who reigned around 521-486 BC, a time when several Persian kings succeeded one another.
H1868G.origine: The name Darius comes from Persian and literally means "lord" or "master." It is a royal Persian title borne by several rulers of ancient Persia. In the Scriptures, this name appears in Aramaic (דָּֽרְיָ֫וֶשׁ), reflecting the influence of Persian administration on the language of official documents during the time of the return from exile.
H1868G.emploi: Darius appears nine times in the book of Ezra, entirely concentrated in chapters 4 to 6 which recount the events of the return from exile. He is presented as a Persian king who, although living far from Jerusalem, plays a decisive role in the restoration of the temple. The Jews report to King Darius (Ezra 5:6-7), he orders an investigation into the archives (Ezra 6:1), then he decides to actively support the project by financing the work and threatening punishment against anyone who would hinder this work (Ezra 6:12). His authorization and protection allow for the completion of the temple (Ezra 6:14-15).
H1868G.portee: The story of Darius shows how God governs history even through foreign kings to fulfill his promises. Despite oppression and obstacles, the Lord watches over his people and raises, at the right moment, a political authority that favors the restoration of his worship. It is a lesson in trust: God never abandons his own, even in exile.

sens: King of Babylon who succeeded Belshazzar
Persian king who founded the Persian-Aryan dynasty
Persian king contemporary with Nehemiah
H1868H.detail:
1. Darius the Mede is the king who seized the Babylonian kingdom at the death of Belshazzar, probably the same figure as King Astyages of the Medes; he organized the administration of the kingdom by establishing one hundred twenty satraps (Daniel 5:31; 6:1).
2. Darius son of Hystaspes is the founder of the great Persian-Aryan dynasty, which reigned around 521 BC; he is a historical king known from Persian archaeology.
3. Darius II or Darius III refer to other Persian kings from later periods: Darius II (also called Nothus) reigned during the time of Nehemiah, and Darius III was the last king of Persia, defeated by Alexander the Great.
H1868H.origine: The name Darius means "lord" in Persian; it is a prestigious royal title borne by several sovereigns of the Persian empire, which explains why the Bible mentions several kings by this name. Persian and Greek historical sources attest to the existence and exploits of these kings.
H1868H.emploi: The name Darius appears six times in the book of Daniel, all in chapter 6 and in chapter 5 (verse 31). The six occurrences concern Darius the Mede: Daniel describes how this king established an organized administration of the kingdom (one hundred twenty satraps), how he issued a decree, and how the prophet Daniel prospered under his reign as well as under that of Cyrus the Persian (Daniel 6:28). These accounts portray Darius as a powerful king but susceptible to the intrigues of his advisors.

sens: To walk on, crush underfoot
To traverse a region, cross it
To draw a bow by bending it with the foot
To lead someone, show them the way
To accomplish a journey, follow a path
H1869.detail:
1. To walk on or crush with the foot: the primary image is that of the foot pressing down, crushing. In Jeremiah 51:33, Babylon is compared to a threshing floor that is trampled at harvest time — grain is trodden to separate it from the chaff. This can be violent: fierce beasts did not tread the path of Job (Job 28:8), meaning they did not venture there.

2. To traverse a land, to take possession by walking on it: when God promises Joshua that every place he sets his foot will be given to him (Joshua 1:3), it means he will cross and dominate that land. Deuteronomy 11:24 reiterates this image.

3. To draw a bow: this more technical meaning appears among archers who bend their bow by treading on it to string it. In Lamentations 2:4, the Lord treads (stretches) His bow like an enemy.

4. To lead, guide someone on a path: a figurative sense of the verb. Psalm 107:7 states that God leads the exiles along the right path, and Isaiah 48:17 promises that the Lord will teach the ways.

5. To walk, follow a path or way: the path of peace that is trodden in Isaiah 59:8 is the way that one travels, that one follows. It is simply to journey, to progress.
H1869.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that depicts the action of the foot: to tread, to walk, to crush. It is linked to the physical image of a step, of movement on the ground. The Hebrew family includes words that speak of path, road (derived from the same root), and movement. The word always evokes a contact of the feet with the ground, whether gentle (to traverse) or violent (to crush).
H1869.emploi: This verb is very common in the Hebrew Bible (59 occurrences) and appears everywhere: in the laws of Deuteronomy, in history (Joshua, Judges, Samuel), in poetry (Psalms, Job, Proverbs), and among the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos, etc.). In its primary and concrete sense, it denotes the action of walking or crushing: soldiers who trod the grapes during the harvest (Judges 9:27), the harvest that is trodden (Jeremiah 48:33). In a figurative sense, it enriches: leading His people (Psalm 107:7), drawing His bow (Psalms 7:13, 11:2), traversing a promised land. Isaiah uses this verb to depict the Lord walking among the nations (Isaiah 63:2-3). The context always clarifies whether the emphasis is on physical action or on dominion, direction, or the path taken.
H1869.portee: This verb invites the Christian reader to meditate on two aspects of their life. First, the image of the trodden path reminds that a disciple does not remain passive: they walk, they progress, they advance (Psalm 119:35: "I will run in the way of your commandments"). Secondly, the idea that God leads, that He Himself treads the path before us, comforts those who feel lost: God does not abandon His people; He guides them to a safe dwelling.

sens: Path, road, itinerary to be traveled
Distance to cover, journey
Manner of acting, conduct, way of life
Habit, custom, usual practice
Moral orientation, spiritual character
Course, accomplishment of an action
H1870G.detail:
1. The way is primarily a physical path or road, an itinerary that one travels on foot or follows. This is the most concrete meaning of the word (Jeremiah 42:3: "the way we should go").
2. By extension, the way refers to the distance to be covered, the journey itself — what one must traverse to go from one point to another.
3. Very often in the Bible, the word shifts to a moral sense: the way becomes the manner of acting, the conduct, the way of life one adopts. One "walks" in a moral way just as one walks on a road (2 Kings 8:27: "He walked in the way of the house of Ahab").
4. The way can also refer to a habit, a custom, a practice that one regularly repeats — the way someone normally behaves.
5. Spiritually, the way refers to the moral or spiritual path one follows: it is good or bad depending on whether one obeys God or not (Proverbs 4:19: "The way of the wicked is like darkness"). God "shows sinners the way" (Psalms 25:8).
6. Finally, the way can denote the accomplishment or course of an action (Genesis 6:12: "all flesh had corrupted its way" means that everyone was leading a corrupt life).
H1870G.origine: The Hebrew word דֶרֶךְ (derekh) comes from a root that evokes the idea of walking, advancing. It has no certain etymology in Hebrew, but it belongs to a family of words related to movement and progression. The word is very ancient and fundamental in biblical thought: it is found everywhere, from the beginning of Genesis to the end of the historical books. Its semantic evolution from physical meaning (path) to moral meaning (conduct) is typical: the Hebrews often thought of moral life as a walk, a trajectory to follow.
H1870G.emploi: The word דֶרֶךְ appears more than 300 times in the Old Testament. It is ubiquitous in the historical books (Genesis, Exodus, 1-2 Kings, 1-2 Chronicles), in the Psalms and Proverbs, and in the prophets. In its concrete sense, it is found in contexts of travel or movement. But very quickly, it is the moral sense that dominates: the "way of someone" is their manner of living, of behaving. God asks His people to "walk in His ways," meaning to obey His commandments and live according to His will. The kings of Israel and Judah are judged based on whether they "walk in the way of the Lord" or "in the way of idols" (1 Kings 11:33, 2 Kings 8:27). In the Psalms and Proverbs, the way is the path of wisdom or folly, of righteousness or sin.
H1870G.portee: For the believer, this word reminds that spiritual life is not a fleeting moment or feeling, but a path, a walk that lasts. God "shows the way" to those who seek it: the Christian is invited to ask God to lead them, to show them the path to follow (Psalms 25:8, Jeremiah 42:3). The word also calls for vigilance: there is a wide way and a narrow way, a way of life and a way of death. It is a powerful image to understand that our daily choices, our habits, our general conduct constitute the path we walk spiritually.

sens: Path traced on the earth, road taken on foot or while traveling
Direction, itinerary to be followed
Manner of living, conducting oneself, believing
H1870H.detail:
1. The word first designates a concrete path, a physical road: in Isaiah 35:8, the "holy way" is a real, cleared, and prepared path where travelers can advance without risk of getting lost.
2. By extension, "way" takes on the meaning of direction to follow or itinerary: it is the path one must take, the orientation one must adopt.
3. Finally, in a very important figurative sense in the Bible, "way" means the manner of living, the moral and spiritual conduct: one speaks of "the way of the Lord" or "the right way" to designate a mode of life that is just and faithful.
H1870H.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of walking, moving. The word "derech" is one of the main ways in Hebrew to speak of the path or journey, and it applies naturally to both material roads and moral and spiritual paths. It is a very rich image: one who follows a way progresses, while one who departs from it goes astray.
H1870H.emploi: The word appears only once in the provided French translation, in Isaiah 35:8, in a context of restoration and protection: God creates a "holy way" where the impure cannot enter and where even the foolish will not go astray. This passage illustrates how the Bible uses "way" to speak not only of a physical road but especially of a protected and sacred path, reserved for the people of God. It is a path of salvation and spiritual security.
H1870H.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites reflection on their own "way": what direction is their life taking? Are they following the way of the Lord, marked by holiness and faithfulness, or are they going astray? The text from Isaiah reassures those who walk on this holy way: they will not go astray; they will be protected. It is a word of encouragement for those who desire to follow God.

sens: main road or official route controlled by the king
direct and established itinerary followed by travelers
land passage or corridor crossing a territory
H1870I.detail:
1. The "royal road" is the main thoroughfare of a kingdom, often maintained and monitored by royal authority. It is an official route, distinct from smaller paths or shortcuts. When the Israelites request to pass through the territory of the Amorites, they promise to follow this royal road precisely, without deviating into fields or vineyards (Numbers 20:17).
2. This road is also the established and well-known route taken by caravans and regular travelers. It is a recognized and permanent path, not an improvisation. By staying on the royal road, the Israelites submitted to a prescribed, visible, and controllable journey by the king of the land they were crossing.
3. More broadly, it is a land passage or corridor that connects regions and that any people must take to travel from one end of the country to the other without causing damage or disturbance.
H1870I.origine: The Hebrew word "derekh" (דרך) literally means "way" or "path." Combined with "melekh" (מלך), which means "king," the expression "derekh melekh" thus refers to the "way of the king" or the "royal road" — the main artery of the land. This expression reflects the ancient geography of the kingdoms of the Levant, where such strategic roads connected major centers and were controlled by the ruling power.
H1870I.emploi: This expression appears twice in the Old Testament, both in the book of Numbers, during the Israelites' journey in the desert. In Numbers 20:17 and 21:22, Moses requests permission to pass through the lands of the Amorites (or Edom) and solemnly commits to staying on the royal road, without entering fields, vineyards, or drawing from wells. These two verses are remarkably parallel: they show how a foreign nation must traverse a kingdom — by the official route, without encroaching on the resources or lands of the king. The context is one of respecting borders and diplomacy between peoples.
H1870I.portee: This expression reveals how God teaches His people to respect established authorities and the borders of others. The Israelites acknowledge the legitimacy of the Amorite territory and accept its conditions: to follow the designated path, not to plunder, and to remain within the outlined framework. For the Christian, this is a lesson on respecting social order and the rights of others, even when traveling in foreign lands. It also shows that God calls His people to transparency and honesty in their dealings with other nations.

sens: Concrete path taken to go from one place to another
Course of a journey, distance to cover
Geographical direction or spatial orientation
Course or direction followed by events
Way of life, moral or spiritual conduct
H1870J.detail:
1. The simplest meaning is that of a physical path, the road taken: it is the trail, the passage through which one moves. In 1 Samuel 9:6, the servant speaks of the "way we must take" to consult a man of God — it refers to the concrete road to follow to reach the destination.
2. The way also refers to a journey, a route, with the idea of travel and distance. Deuteronomy 2:1 mentions the wanderings of Israel in the desert: it is the path traveled, the sequence of movements.
3. The word can simply indicate a direction or spatial orientation: "eastern" (Ezekiel 40:10) comes from this — literally "from the side of the rising sun." It points to where? in what direction?
4. "Way" extends to the course of life, to the succession of events: Job 28:23 speaks of the way of wisdom, as the path it follows, the course it takes.
5. Finally, the term applies to moral and spiritual conduct: one speaks of a person's way to signify their way of life, their choices, their ethical orientation.
H1870J.origine: The Hebrew word derech comes from a root evoking the idea of walking, of moving. It belongs to a family of words related to locomotion and movement. In the Greek Old Testament, it is often translated by the Greek "hodos," which carries the same nuances: the concrete path, the journey, but also, in a more figurative sense, the course of life or conduct.
H1870J.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in biblical Hebrew, used about sixty times in the historical, wisdom, and prophetic books. It appears in accounts of movements (Joshua, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel) to describe the routes taken by characters. It also appears massively in Ezekiel (forty-one times!) to designate the orientations of the different doors and chambers of the temple; there, it simply indicates a spatial direction. In the wisdom books like Job, the term acquires depth: it evokes the direction of life, the way of wisdom that only God knows (Job 28:23). Its meaning thus constantly nuances: from geometric and spatial sense to existential and moral sense.
H1870J.portee: The word "way" invites the believer to meditate on their spiritual direction. In the Bible, God "knows the way" (Job 28:23), while man must learn to walk in the right way. It is a powerful image for divine guidance and human responsibility: life is not chaos, but a journey that can be oriented toward good or evil, a path where God can guide us if we accept His direction.

sens: Path or trace that one follows on foot or while traveling from one place to another
Itinerary of a journey, distance to be covered
Direction or side towards which one is going
Manner of acting, being, habit or conduct
Way of life, moral or spiritual orientation
Course or unfolding (of an action, an event)
H1870K.detail:
1. The way is primarily the concrete path on which one walks or travels: a road, a trail, a passage marked on the ground. It is the place through which one passes to go from one location to another (Genesis 3:24: the way to the tree of life).
2. By extension, the word designates the journey itself, the distance to be covered, or the journey in its entirety. The context of Deuteronomy 1:33 shows God guiding Israel on the road through the desert, showing the way to follow.
3. The way can also simply indicate a direction, the road to take: "By what way shall we go up?" is asked in 2 Kings 3:8.
4. Figuratively, the way represents the manner of doing, the habit, the behavior: how one acts, how one leads their life. Proverbs 7:8 speaks of the "way" or direction someone takes in their conduct.
5. The way also evokes the course of moral and spiritual life: the path one follows before God, our ethical and religious choices, what defines our character and values.
6. More broadly, it is the course of things, the unfolding of an action or event: the way that life, history, or the will of God takes.
H1870K.origine: The Hebrew word דֶּרֶךְ (derèkh) comes from a root expressing the idea of following, walking, progressing. Its primary image is that of a trace, a path that one follows to advance. Like many biblical words, it has gradually enriched its meaning: from the very concrete sense of physical path, it has come to designate any journey (a trip, a direction), then any manner of proceeding (a method, a behavior, a moral orientation). It is a fundamental word in the Hebrew Bible, omnipresent in speaking about the relationship between man and God: the way of the righteous or the wicked.
H1870K.emploi: The word דֶּרֶךְ appears 123 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the historical and wisdom books. It initially designates the concrete paths of the desert (Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy): the roads that Israel must take to reach the Promised Land, guided by God. In the historical books (Samuel, Kings), it often remains literal: we speak of paths to take, roads to watch over. But gradually, especially in Proverbs and Psalms, the meaning becomes moral: the way of the righteous, the way of the wicked, the path that God asks to follow. The word thus encompasses both the concrete (a path, a road) and the figurative (a conduct, a way of life, an orientation before God). Even in historical passages, this dual dimension appears: a way is never purely physical; it also symbolizes a life choice.
H1870K.portee: For the Christian, the word way evokes the central question: what path am I on? Where am I going? The Bible constantly speaks of the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked, inviting everyone to examine their own moral direction. The way also reminds us that spiritual life is not a fixed point, but a walk, a progress, a progression. Following the way of God means accepting His guidance and directives. It is a word that invites awareness, vigilance, and alignment with divine will.

sens: Path, trail, physical trace by which one moves
Route, journey, distance to cover during a move
Direction, orientation towards a place or goal
Manner of acting, conduct, way of living
Course of life, destiny, existential trajectory
Moral character, habitual disposition of the heart
H1870L.detail:
1. The way in the concrete sense is primarily a road, a trail, the physical path by which one travels: Genesis 19:2 speaks of continuing one's "way" after leaving a house; it is the trace one takes to go from one place to another.
2. The way also designates the journey itself, the distance to be covered: Exodus 23:20 mentions an angel who protects "on the way," that is, during the movement, the journey being accomplished.
3. It can indicate a direction, a course, an orientation: in Deuteronomy 28:68, God brings Israel "on the way" to Egypt; it is the imposed direction, the sense of the journey.
4. In the moral and psychological sense, the way becomes the manner of acting, the conduct: Proverbs 16:9 states that "the heart meditates on its way," meaning that a person thinks about their way of living, their behavior.
5. The way also figures the course of a life, the destiny: it is the overall trajectory one travels, the entirety of a life's path.
6. Finally, the way can represent moral character, the deep orientation of the heart: it is less about isolated acts than about habitual orientation, what the heart naturally leans towards, its disposition.
H1870L.origine: The Hebrew word דֶּרֶךְ (derekh) comes from a root that evokes the idea of walking, moving. It is related to other words in the Semitic family that also mean "way" or "road." The basic image is that of a path trodden underfoot, the trace left by those who pass. This word is very ancient and very common in Hebrew; it is used for both literal paths and the figurative trajectories of life and morality.
H1870L.emploi: The word appears 146 times in the Old Testament, making it one of the most frequent terms. It is found everywhere: in travel narratives (Genesis 24 with Abraham's servant traveling), in divine instructions (Exodus 23:20 where God sends His angel on the way), and in wisdom literature (Proverbs 16:9 about the direction of life). In its early uses, the meaning is concrete and geographical; in Proverbs and the wisdom passages, it becomes metaphorical and denotes a way of life. Even in the laws of Deuteronomy, the "way" can refer to how one conducts oneself (Deuteronomy 8:2: the Lord led Israel "on the way," meaning according to a certain orientation of life and faith). The context determines whether the word speaks of a physical road or a moral trajectory.
H1870L.portee: For the Christian reader, this word highlights that God does not abandon His children along the way: He "protects on the way" (Exodus 23:20). It also emphasizes that our life is not a succession of isolated acts, but a coherent journey of which God knows and guides every step. Finally, it invites reflection on the "way" we follow: not only where we are going, but how we live, what our moral and spiritual direction is.

sens: Persian gold coin
Unit of weight and economic value
Voluntary contribution or offering
H1871.detail:
1. The darique is a gold coin issued by the Persian Empire, valued at 128 grains of gold (approximately 8.32 grams). It circulated in Palestine after the return from exile, during the reconstruction of the Temple. It is a prestigious currency, used in significant exchanges and official transactions.

2. The term also refers to a unit of measure of economic value, allowing for the evaluation of wealth or contributions. When Ezra mentions "sixty-one thousand dariques of gold" given to the Temple treasury, he quantifies a considerable wealth using this standardized unit (Ezra 2:69).

3. In the accounts of reconstruction, the darique becomes a symbol of the generous offerings that family leaders and the people give to rebuild the Temple and the holy work. Nehemiah 7:70-72 shows massive contributions in dariques: the governor alone gives a thousand, the family leaders twenty thousand, and the rest of the people twenty thousand more, revealing the financial commitment of the restored people.
H1871.origine: The Hebrew word darcemon (דַּרְכְּמוֹן) is borrowed from Old Persian and reflects the influence of the Persian Empire on the economy of Judah after the exile in 586 BC. The term enters Late Biblical Hebrew because this coin, minted under the Achaemenids, becomes the main monetary instrument for trade and official life. It is a real and historical currency, archaeologically attested.
H1871.emploi: The word darique appears only four times in the Bible, exclusively in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, which recount the return from exile and the reconstruction of the Temple (586-445 BC). These four occurrences are concentrated in two parallel passages: Ezra 2:69 and Nehemiah 7:70-72. In these two contexts, the darique measures the massive contributions made by the Persian authorities, family leaders, and the entire people to finance the Temple works. The word illustrates both the scale of the restoration effort and the generosity of the donors: the amounts mentioned represent considerable wealth. The darique thus symbolizes the contribution of all levels of the restored Jewish society to this sacred project.
H1871.portee: The darique reminds us that the reconstruction of the Temple was not free: it required massive resources, mobilized by the people and their leaders. This concrete economic detail invites the Christian reader to reflect on what it truly costs to build a holy work, and on the importance of material sacrifice and generous giving in the service of God. It is also a testimony to the faithfulness of the people who, emerging from exile, commit wholeheartedly to the restoration of worship.

sens: The limb of the body that extends from the shoulder to the hand
Instrument of strength, power, or action
Ability to act or accomplish
H1872.detail:
1. The arm is the limb that extends from the shoulder to the hand, allowing for grasping, holding, and manipulating. In Nebuchadnezzar's vision in Daniel 2:32, the arms of the statue, made of silver, literally represent this part of the body.
2. Figuratively, the "arm" symbolizes the strength, the power of action of a person or a force. This is why the statue in Daniel, composed of different metals from top to bottom, uses the arm as a structural element: it embodies the power and capacity of the kingdom it represents.
3. In the Bible, "the arm" can more broadly refer to the ability to act, to intervene, to accomplish one's will — notably the arm of God, a symbol of His powerful intervention.
H1872.origine: This Aramaic word דְּרַע (de.ra) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word זְרוֹעַ (ze.ro.a), which literally means "arm." Aramaic and Hebrew share common roots, and this word appears in many biblical contexts to denote the limb of the body, but also, figuratively, the acting power.
H1872.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in Aramaic, in the context of Nebuchadnezzar's prophetic vision in Daniel 2:32. This vision describes a great statue composed of different metals: gold for the head, silver for the chest and arms, bronze for the belly and thighs, and iron mixed with clay for the feet. The silver arms, placed after the head and chest, mark a transition in the quality and weight of the materials, symbolizing the progressive decline of the kingdoms represented by the statue.
H1872.portee: This prophetic vision teaches the reader how God views the history of human kingdoms: not as an endless progression, but as a succession of declining powers, from the strongest to the most fragile. The arm, as an instrument of strength, reminds us that all earthly power, however formidable, is measured and limited in God's plan.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Zerah
H1873.detail: Dara is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:6. He is the son of Zerah and the brother of Zimri, Ethan, Heman, and Calcol — five sons famous for their wisdom according to biblical tradition. His name appears in the genealogy of Judah, which traces the main lineages of the people before the establishment of the Israelite monarchy.
H1873.origine: The name Dara means "the arm" in Hebrew, evoking strength and power. This name fits within the tradition of names in the family of Zerah, who himself bears a name meaning "rising sun" or "dawn." The genealogy in which Dara appears belongs to the genealogical records of Judah preserved in the book of Chronicles.
H1873.emploi: Dara is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:6, in the list of the sons of Zerah. This very brief mention places him among the descendants of Judah in the pre-monarchic period. His brothers, particularly Ethan and Heman, are associated with wisdom in other parts of Scripture, but Dara himself is not the subject of other biblical narratives or teachings. He represents a figure in the genealogy of Judah whose name and kinship are known.

sens: Head of a family of temple servants returning from exile
H1874.detail: Darkon is the name of a man who lived during the time of the exile and the return to Jerusalem. He was the head of a family of temple servants (called "Nethinim") who had been deported to Babylon and who returned with Zerubbabel to rebuild the temple. His name appears in the official lists of those who participated in the return.
H1874.origine: The Hebrew name Darkon literally means "scatterer" (one who disperses). It comes from a root that evokes the action of scattering or dispersing. This type of descriptive name was common in Israel.
H1874.emploi: Darkon is mentioned exactly twice in the Bible, in two almost identical lists: first in Ezra 2:56 among the families of temple servants who returned from exile with Zerubbabel, and then in Nehemiah 7:58 in a similar list. These two passages record the same families, and Darkon appears each time alongside the sons of Jaala and the sons of Guiddel, all heads of houses of temple servants.

sens: to inquire of someone or go consult them, notably a prophet or diviner
to address God through prayer and worship, to seek Him with all one's heart
to demand insistently, to claim, to require
to investigate something, to inquire to discover the truth
to search for or pursue something diligently and carefully
H1875.detail:
1. To inquire of someone or go consult them: this means to approach a person reputed to have answers, notably a prophet or diviner. In 1 Kings 22:8, the king desires to consult a prophet to know God's will regarding a battle. The word describes the act of approaching someone to ask for advice or revelation.

2. To address God through prayer and worship: this is the most frequent meaning in the Bible. Seeking God means to sincerely search for Him with all one's heart and soul, through prayer and worship. In 2 Chronicles 15:12, the Israelites commit to seek the Lord, their God. It is a voluntary act of drawing closer to the divine.

3. To demand insistently, to claim, to require: the word can also mean to claim something in justice or law. In Genesis 9:5, God declares that He will require (claim in justice) the blood of men. It expresses a legitimate and irrevocable demand.

4. To investigate something, to inquire to discover the truth: this means to search for facts, to conduct an inquiry or judgment. The word describes the action of scrutinizing, examining closely to establish the truth.

5. To search for or pursue something diligently and carefully: this means to seek with diligence and attention, putting in effort, as one does for an important possession or knowledge. The word emphasizes perseverance and commitment in the search.
H1875.origine: The verb darash comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of digging, exploring, searching while engaging physically and mentally. The starting image is that of someone walking back and forth, digging to find. This verb belongs to the family of Hebrew words related to quest and investigation. It stands in contrast to indifference: to seek is to make an effort, to actively engage in a process.
H1875.emploi: Darash appears 152 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the Histories (Kings, Chronicles) and in the Psalms. The word is first used to describe the action of consulting God, a prophet, or a diviner (1 Kings 22:8; 2 Kings 1:2-16), then to express the sincere search for God in prayer and worship (2 Chronicles 15:12; Ezra 6:21), which becomes its most spiritual usage. It also denotes God's demand for accountability regarding the blood shed (Genesis 9:5). In the Psalms, the verb invites to seek God with perseverance (Psalms 105:4). Its meaning thus varies from the most concrete (consulting someone) to the most intimate (seeking God with all one's heart).
H1875.portee: This word reveals that biblical faith is not passive: seeking God is an act, a decision, a voluntary process that requires energy and a whole heart. The Bible constantly encourages the believer to seek God, through prayer, the study of His Word, and obedience. Darash also shows us that God wants to be found and consulted by His people; He invites this quest. It is a call to a living relationship with Him.

sens: to make plants grow from seeds
to grow green
to produce new vegetation
H1876.detail:
1. The word describes the action of a seed that germinates and pushes up from the ground: it is the moment when new life emerges from the soil. In Genesis 1:11, God commands the earth to bring forth vegetation, plants, and fruit trees — this is the beginning of all plant life.
2. It can also refer to growing green and strong, to be covered with foliage and greenery. In Joel 2:22, the pastures are covered with greenery after the drought and the devastation of locusts: life returns to the devastated land.
3. Figuratively, the word evokes any renewal, any rebirth of hope or fertility after a period of sterility or death.
H1876.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes the idea of greenness and growth. The simple form (Qal) means that the plant itself germinates; the causative form (Hiphil) means that someone or something (here, the earth obeying God) causes the germination. The image is that of the grain awakening to life underground and pushing toward the light.
H1876.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible. The first time, in Genesis 1:11, it expresses God's creative command: "Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after its kind" — it is an act of obedience of creation to the word of God. The second time, in Joel 2:22, it describes restoration: after the judgment by locusts, the pastures germinate again, and the trees bear their fruit. The word thus marks both the mystery of initial creation and the promise of divine restoration.
H1876.portee: This word reminds the believer that life and fertility come from God alone. In Genesis, it shows God's creative omnipotence; in Joel, it comforts by revealing that God destroys only to restore, that after judgment comes renewal. It is a word of hope: even what seems dead can germinate again under God's hand.

sens: the young grass that grows in fields and pastures
the tender green cover, especially what is born in spring
that which is fragile, ephemeral, destined to dry and disappear
the biblical image of human fragility compared to the grass of the fields
H1877.detail: 1. Greenery primarily refers to the fresh and new grass that covers the earth after rains, the young tender vegetation that naturally grows in fields and pastures. In Genesis 1:11, God tells the earth to produce "greenery," grass yielding seed — this is the creation of the simplest plant kingdom, which nourishes animals. 2. The word particularly evokes the green cover of spring, this fresh and living grass that re-greens after winter or the arrival of rain: in Psalms 23:2, the Lord leads His people to "green pastures." 3. But the Bible also uses this word to emphasize fragility: the grass is tender, it dries quickly, it is cut down in an instant. In Psalms 37:2, the wicked "are cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb." 4. This fragility becomes a powerful image: men are like grass that passes, perishable and brief. In Isaiah 37:27, the trembling enemies are "like tender grass," without strength or duration — the image says: they are nothing.
H1877.origine: The Hebrew word dèsha comes from a root that refers to the idea of growth and greening. It specifically designates new grass, young vegetation, in contrast to trees or crops. Aramaic uses a very similar word (détha): the same reality, the same plant, but in the language of the people from the Exile. It is a simple word, part of everyday vocabulary, rooted in the observation of nature.
H1877.emploi: The word appears fourteen times in the Old Testament, mostly in poetic passages and in the law. It first appears in the creation narrative (Genesis 1), where it names the first type of plant created. It is found in Deuteronomy 32:2, where the Word of God falls on the greenery like rain. It also appears in the Psalms and Isaiah, almost always with a nuance of fragility: the wicked, the enemies of Israel, are compared to grass that dries, that is cut down. In Job 38:27, God questions: it is He who "makes the grass to germinate and come forth" — an image of His omnipotence. The word thus transitions from the concrete meaning (the grass seen) to the figurative meaning (the fragility of human life).
H1877.portee: This word invites the reader to contemplate simple creation and to see both God's goodness (who provides for the nourishment of animals and men) and His call to humility: we are all like grass, transient and fragile. It is a reminder that our life depends entirely on God, and that our true solidity is not in ourselves, but in His Word which remains eternally. Greenery says: enjoy the present, be grateful, do not be proud.

sens: To become fat, to grow, to fatten oneself
To prosper, to become rich, to be satisfied
To anoint with oil, to coat with fat
To make fat, to cause to prosper
To remove the ashes (from the altar)
To find acceptable, to approve (an offering)
H1878.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to become fat or to grow, like an animal that is well-fed (Deuteronomy 31:20 describes the people who become fat when they eat their fill in the promised land).

2. The word shifts to a figurative meaning: to prosper spiritually or materially, to enjoy abundance. The generous soul "will be satisfied" (Proverbs 11:25): it enjoys the fruits of its generosity.

3. To anoint with oil means to rub the body or head with fatty oil: in Psalms 23:5, the Lord "anoints my head with oil," an act of honor and care.

4. The Hebrew Piel "makes fat" or "causes to prosper": it is a voluntary action that enriches or favors someone.

5. At the altar, the priest "removes the ashes" (Numbers 4:13): he takes away the fatty and burnt residues of the sacrifice to maintain the altar.

6. Finally, God "approves" an offering (Psalms 20:4), meaning He accepts it favorably; some scholars see a connection here with the fatty portions of the sacrifice, reserved for the Lord.
H1878.origine: The Hebrew word ḏāšēn comes from a root that means "fat" or "grease." Fat is a symbol of strength, wealth, and life in the Bible (the best part of the sacrificial animal). The same word can evoke the anointing oil, which makes the skin greasy, smooth, and shiny. The main verb (Qal) first means "to become fat," then "to prosper" in a figurative sense; other verbal forms vary the subject (to cause others to prosper, to remove fatty ashes, etc.).
H1878.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Old Testament, mostly in Psalms and Proverbs. In Deuteronomy 31:20, it describes the people who become fat from abundant food and forget God. In Psalms and Proverbs, "to become fat" or "to be satisfied" becomes a metaphor for spiritual prosperity or happiness (Psalms 23:5, Proverbs 11:25). In worship contexts (Exodus, Numbers), the verb refers to the removal of the fatty ashes from the altar or God's approval of a sacrifice. The word changes meaning depending on the context: a warning cry (forgetting God despite abundance), a promise of blessing (being satisfied with good), or a detail of Temple service (managing fatty remains and ashes).
H1878.portee: This word reminds the believer that material prosperity is a gift from God, but also a trap: the people of Israel become fat and turn away from their God. It invites seeking true satisfaction in the presence and kindness of the Lord (Psalms 23), rather than in material goods alone. The anointing with oil evokes God's personal and honoring attention towards His people, an act of intimacy and grace.

sens: Having strength, power, physical vigor
Rich, abundant, fertile (referring to the land or its products)
Having weight, importance, authority
H1879.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes physical strength, robustness: a powerful and vigorous person. In Psalms 22:30, the "mighty of the earth" are those who have the power and strength to bow down before God.
2. It then applies to the richness and abundance of the land or plants: a fertile and generous land yields tasty fruits. In Isaiah 30:23, the bread produced by the land will be "delicious," meaning rich, nourishing, full of sap.
3. A living being can be vigorous in the sense of being full of life, youth, and health: in Psalms 92:15, the righteous "still bear fruit in old age" because they are "full of sap and green," meaning filled with a vital force that does not wear out.
H1879.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of fat, thick, abundant. Fat, in biblical thought, symbolizes strength, wealth, and fullness. From the same family, there are words designating the ashes of fat animals (the purest part of the sacrifice) or prosperity. This image of fat as strength and abundance runs throughout the Bible.
H1879.emploi: The word appears three times in the provided usages, each time nuanced. In Psalms 22:30, it qualifies the powerful men of the earth. In Isaiah 30:23, it describes the bread produced by a land that God waters: a rich and nourishing bread. In Psalms 92:15, it characterizes the enduring youth of the righteous, a vital force that persists even in old age. The word thus oscillates between human power (political or military), the richness of creation (the generous land), and the spiritual vitality of the believer.
H1879.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that true strength does not come from the flesh or human wealth, but from God. The righteous who cling to Him remain vigorous and fruitful, even in the decline of life. It is a promise: whoever finds their source in God remains rich in life and fruit, regardless of age or circumstances.

sens: Gray residue left by fire after combustion
Fat from sacrificed victims, mixed with the ashes of the altar
Abundance, wealth, fertility of the land or divine blessings
H1880.detail:
1. Ash is the gray residue left by fire when it consumes a sacrifice. The priests were to remove this ash from the altar and place it beside it (Leviticus 6:3), in a reserved place to the east (Leviticus 1:16). This is an act of ritual service, marking the end of the burnt offering.

2. The word also refers to the fat mixed with the ashes: in the burnt offerings, the fat of the victim burned with the rest, creating these "fatty ashes" that ascended to heaven. This is why the olive tree can say it renounces its "oil" (its precious fat) to honor God (Judges 9:9).

3. By extension, "ash" means abundance, fertility, wealth — like the rich and fertile land that yields beautiful harvests. Psalm 65:12 says that God's "paths" "drip with abundance": His blessings fall on the land like a generous rain that fills it with good things. This image expresses divine generosity that fills His creatures.
H1880.origine: The Hebrew word primarily denotes the material ash from fire. But because of its mixture with fat in the sacrifice (the richest and most precious part), the term has taken on the meaning of wealth and fullness. In the Greek Bible (Septuagint), the same word ἱλαστήριον and its derivatives for "expiation" retain this idea of what ascends to God. The link between ash and abundance comes from the idea that what burns on the altar — particularly the fat — ascends to heaven like a pleasant aroma, a symbol of divine blessing.
H1880.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible. In the books of Leviticus, it almost always refers to the ash from burnt offerings to be removed from the altar — it is a precise task of worship. In Psalms and prophecy (Psalms 36:9, 65:12, Isaiah 55:2, Jeremiah 31:14), the meaning shifts towards abundance, wealth, delicious foods, fertility: it is the divine blessing that satisfies and fills with His goods. Judges 9:9 uses "oil" as close to the word "ash" to speak of what is precious and life-giving. This transition in meaning shows how the imagery of sacrifice (what ascends to God and returns as blessing) has nourished the poetic language of faith.
H1880.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that our offerings ascend to God — whether they be prayers, service, or self-denial — and that God responds by pouring out His abundance. The ashes of the altar are not a loss, but the passage to blessing. It is an invitation to trust: giving to God is receiving from Him what truly satisfies and enriches the soul.

sens: Divine prescription or rule established by a legitimate authority
Decree or ordinance of a king or civil authority
Set of rules and customs governing a community
H1881.detail:
1. The law is primarily what God has prescribed for His people — the divine teaching that guides life and relationship with Him. In Deuteronomy 33:2, Moses celebrates "the fire of the law" that the Lord gave from Sinai: it is the major gift from the God who revealed Himself to Israel.

2. The word also designates any decree or official ordinance of a king or recognized authority. When Ahasuerus promulgates his edict in Esther 3:14, this decree is called dat — it is a command endowed with authority that binds all subjects of the kingdom and "must be published in every province."

3. More broadly, a dat is a rule, a custom, an established and recognized practice within a community. In Esther 1:13, the king's wise men who "knew the laws and the right" are those who master the rules of protocol and governance. This word can also simply refer to the established order — the way things must be done.
H1881.origine: The Hebrew word dat comes from a root meaning "to arrange, order, establish." It fundamentally designates what is established and set, what has the force of a rule. It is the same word found in Aramaic (dat, H1882): it naturally passed into the administrative language of the Persian empire mentioned in the book of Esther. A word from the same family is dabar ("word," "thing"), as the law or edict is primarily a spoken word that produces an order.
H1881.emploi: This word appears 21 times in the Old Testament, primarily in two contexts: first in Deuteronomy 33:2, where Moses speaks of the law revealed by God at Sinai — the moment when Israel received the Torah. Then, the word dominates the book of Esther (17 occurrences), where it designates the edicts of the Persian king (Ahasuerus) that are intertwined and govern the life of the entire empire and the Jewish people. These royal edicts are presented as irrevocable and absolute: according to Esther 1:19, the "law of the Medes and Persians" cannot be abrogated. The contrast is striking: the divine law of Sinai opposes love and liberation, while the edicts of the Persian king in Esther are often instruments of threat and death — before God overturns them into salvation for His people.
H1881.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader grasp the biblical tension between authority: God's law is the gift of love that guides to true life, while human laws, even those of great empires, remain fragile and can serve evil. Through Esther, the Bible shows that even when the edicts of power seem all-powerful, it is God who holds the helm. The Christian learns to respect established authority but recognizes that only God's law — that of love and grace — is truly eternal and salvific.

sens: Decree or command of a king
Set of rules and obligations established by an authority
The law of God, His teaching and commandments
H1882.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a royal decree, that is, an order emanating from the power of the king. In Ezra 7:26, the law of the king is mentioned alongside the law of God: these are two ordinances that must be respected, one coming from the earthly throne, the other from heaven. King Artaxerxes promulgates laws that must be executed without delay.
2. More broadly, the word designates a system of rules and mandatory prescriptions. In Daniel 6:12, we speak of "the law of the Medes and Persians, which is unchangeable": it is the set of norms that govern the kingdom and are imposed on all. These laws are often irreversible and must be strictly followed.
3. The law of God is the teaching and commandments that the Lord has given to His people. In Ezra 7:21, Ezra is described as "well-versed in the law of the God of heaven," which means he deeply knows these commandments and can teach them. In Daniel 6:5, Daniel's adversaries seek an occasion against him "in the law of his God," for Daniel's faith binds him to obey what God commands.
H1882.origine: The Hebrew word dat comes from a root meaning to fix, establish, or set in place. It designates what is established with authority and must remain stable. The context of biblical usages (the books of Ezra and Daniel) shows that this word was particularly used in the context of Persian administration, where royal decrees had the force of immutable law. In late biblical Hebrew, dat applies to both human laws and divine law.
H1882.emploi: The word dat appears 13 times in the Old Testament, concentrated in the books of Ezra and Daniel. It is used to designate the ordinances of the Persian king Artaxerxes (Ezra 7:12, 7:21, 7:26) and the mention of irreversible rules such as "the law of the Medes and Persians" (Daniel 6:12). The word also applies to the law of God (Ezra 7:26; Daniel 6:5), placing on the same level — regarding the obligation of obedience — the commandments of the Lord and those of earthly authorities. These texts show that the dat is a binding prescription, often irrevocable once established, whether it comes from the king or the God of Israel.
H1882.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God has established His commandments with the same authority that a king establishes his decrees, and that obeying God's law is not optional but mandatory. It is also an invitation to respect the distinction between human law and divine law: even though both have the force of obligation, only God's law is absolutely just and perfect. Daniel and Ezra exemplify faithfulness to God's law even when it contradicts the laws of the kingdom in which they live.

sens: Low vegetation that grows in fields and meadows
Food for grazing animals
Figuratively: humble condition devoid of human dignity
H1883.detail:
1. The word designates the herbaceous vegetation that covers fields and meadows — these low and soft plants, different from trees or bushes. In Nebuchadnezzar's dream, the grass of the fields is the setting where the giant tree stood (Daniel 4:15).
2. Grass is the natural food of livestock grazing in pastures. It symbolizes a simple and animal subsistence: "Let him be drenched with the dew of heaven, and let him have, like the beasts, the grass of the earth for his share" (Daniel 4:15).
3. Figuratively, eating the grass of the fields means living like a beast — stripped of human dignity, reduced to an animal state. The king, transformed into an animal, had "the grass of the fields" for food (Daniel 4:23), an image of his complete humiliation and distance from his royal condition.
H1883.origine: This Aramaic word is the direct counterpart of the Hebrew word "deshe" (דֶּ֫שֶׁא, H1877), which also means green grass, greenery. Aramaic and Hebrew share the same root to designate this simple and fragile vegetation that covers the ground. The word evokes the image of tender and ephemeral plants, in contrast to more solid and durable creations.
H1883.emploi: This word appears twice in the Aramaic Bible, exclusively in the book of Daniel, in chapter 4 (verses 15 and 23). Both occurrences are found in the account of Nebuchadnezzar's dream: the king becomes insane and lives like a beast of the field, eating grass. Grass is always mentioned as the share, the food granted to the degraded king — it contrasts with his previous royal condition. The context is one of supernatural humiliation, of divine judgment that reduces a powerful man to a bestial state.
H1883.portee: This word reminds us of the radical humility to which God can reduce the most powerful — not out of cruelty, but to bring them back to wisdom. Grass also symbolizes the fragility of all earthly greatness that rises without recognizing God. For the believer, it is an invitation not to be proud of one's status or strength, but to seek a greatness of another order: one that acknowledges the sovereignty of the eternal God.

sens: Magistrate responsible for administering justice
One who interprets and applies laws and decrees
Court official in the royal administration of an empire
H1884.detail:
1. The judge is a magistrate entrusted with the power to resolve disputes and administer justice. In Babylon, under the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, he holds an official position within the hierarchy of the kingdom.
2. Beyond the judicial function, the judge is one who interprets the decrees of the king and the laws in force, and then applies them. He therefore possesses specialized knowledge and authority to declare the law.
3. In the context of the Babylonian empire in Daniel 3, the judge is a high royal official summoned to the dedication of the statue, alongside governors, treasurers, and other magistrates. It is a title of dignity within the imperial administration, not merely a local function.
H1884.origine: The Aramaic word comes from a Semitic root meaning "to say" or "to judge" — the fundamental idea being that of one who speaks with authority to decide and determine. In the Mesopotamian empires, the title "judge" regularly designates high court magistrates, responsible not only for administering justice but also for interpreting the will of the sovereign.
H1884.emploi: This word appears twice in the Aramaic New Testament — both occurrences are found in Daniel 3:2 and 3:3, where Nebuchadnezzar summons the magistrates of the kingdom to attend the dedication of his golden statue. In these two verses, the judge is listed among the high officials of the Babylonian state. The context shows that it is a prestigious and coveted position, part of the ruling elite of the empire. The term applies here to court officials rather than local judges.
H1884.portee: This word reminds us that in ancient times, as today, justice is an essential cog in the machinery of power. For the reader, it also emphasizes that at the very heart of Babylonian power — before the king's statue — are magistrates and judges who must make a choice: obey the decree of the sovereign or honor the God of Israel. This tension between human authority and God's authority is central to the narrative of Daniel.

sens: Reubenite leader, son of Eliab
Conspirator in Korah's rebellion against Moses and Aaron
H1885.detail:
1. Dathan is a man from the tribe of Reuben, son of Eliab and brother of Abiram and Nemuel. He lived during the time of the Exodus from Egypt and in the wilderness (Numbers 16:1).
2. Dathan joins Korah and his brother Abiram in rebelling against the authority of Moses and Aaron. When Moses calls them, they refuse to come up to him (Numbers 16:12). Korah, Dathan, and Abiram gather a congregation against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 26:9), which triggers divine judgment: Dathan, Abiram, and their families are swallowed up by the earth that opens under their tents (Numbers 16:25-27).
H1885.origine: The name Dathan literally means "belonging to a fountain." It designates a notable from the tribe of Reuben during the time of the Exodus.
H1885.emploi: Dathan appears eight times in the Bible, primarily in Numbers 16 during the rebellion against Moses. His story is also mentioned in Psalm 106:17 as an example of God's judgment. He is always presented alongside Korah and his brother Abiram: first as a participant in the conspiracy, then as a founder of the assembly that rises up against divine leadership, and finally as one who suffers the terrible punishment of being swallowed by the earth with his household.
H1885.portee: The story of Dathan warns believers about the danger of rebellion against the authority that God has established. His revolt, motivated by pride and refusal to submit, leads to destruction. It is a major biblical example of divine judgment on insubordination, reminding us that God takes seriously the respect for the order He establishes among His people.

sens: city in northern Palestine
place where Joseph was sold by his brothers
residence of the prophet Elisha
H1886.detail:
1. Dothan is a city located in northern Palestine, about 19 kilometers north of Samaria. It is known as an important site in the biblical history of the people of Israel.
2. It is at Dothan that Joseph's brothers found him and sold him as a slave: Joseph was searching for his brothers scattered in the fields, and a man told him they had said, "Let us go to Dothan." It is there that he found them (Genesis 37:17).
3. Dothan is also famous as the residence of the prophet Elisha. When the king of Syria wanted to capture him, it was reported to him: "Behold, he is in Dothan" (2 Kings 6:13), which reminds us that the prophet was staying there.
H1886.origine: The name Dothan literally means "two wells," which likely reflects a geographical feature of the place. It is a city name specific to the geography of the ancient Levant.
H1886.emploi: Dothan appears twice in the Bible. First in Genesis 37:17, where it is the setting for the family drama of Joseph: it is there that his brothers sell him into slavery, a pivotal moment in Joseph's story and his descendants. Then in 2 Kings 6:13, where it is associated with the life of the prophet Elisha, showing that it was an important center where the prophets of Israel could reside and carry out their ministry.

sens: Call for attention to present something or someone
Signal of an imminent action or approaching consequence
H1887.detail:
1. This Hebrew word is an interjection that functions like a bell: it tells the reader "attention, look!" to show them something important. In Genesis 47:23, Joseph uses it to present to the people the grain they are about to receive: "behold, here is seed for you." It accompanies the revelation of a present reality or one that unfolds before their eyes.
2. "Behold" can also announce what is to come or what must happen, particularly a consequence or judgment. In Ezekiel 16:43, God introduces imminent punishment with "behold": "behold, I will bring your conduct upon your head." The word creates a break effect, as if God marks a dramatic turning point.
H1887.origine: This interjection comes from ancient Hebrew and has no "root" in the usual sense, as it is a fixed and primitive word, originally intended for exclamation. It belongs to the family of small words that structure living speech: it commands attention, like the word of one who speaks seeks to create an encounter with the one who listens.
H1887.emploi: The word appears twice in the transmitted Hebrew Bible, in the two cited passages. In Genesis 47:23, it is Joseph who uses it to provide the Egyptian people with their sustenance: the tone is pedagogical and benevolent. In Ezekiel 16:43, it is God who employs it to announce the reversal of judgment against Jerusalem: the tone is solemn and fearsome. In both cases, "behold" marks the threshold where what was hidden or absent becomes manifest and real.
H1887.portee: This interjection invites the reader not to remain passive in the face of the words of the Bible. It says: "Be attentive, something is happening, something is being built or overturned before you." For the believer, it reminds us that God speaks directly and that His word brings concrete transformation — blessing or judgment — in real history. It is an invitation to listen with the vigilance of one who knows that every divine word carries weight.

sens: interjection to attract attention
interjection of astonishment or surprise
H1888A.detail:
1. This interjection serves to call someone or to point to something: "Eh, I see four men" (Daniel 3:25). Nebuchadnezzar, the Babylonian king, uses it to direct the attention of those listening to an incredible spectacle: men walking alive in a fiery furnace without being consumed.
2. The word also expresses astonishment at something unexpected or wonderful. Here, it is the king's surprise at this miracle: he expects to see three men burning, and behold, he sees four, one of whom has the appearance of a god.
H1888A.origine: It is an Aramaic word (the language spoken in Babylon), which resembles the Hebrew word "הֵא" (he) with the same meaning: "behold, look." These are very ancient interjections, like hand gestures that say "there!" or "see!".
H1888A.emploi: The word appears only once in Aramaic in the Bible, in Daniel 3:25. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, uses it when he looks at a blazing furnace and witnesses a miracle: God's servants walk unharmed in the fire. It is a decisive moment where the astonished king communicates what he sees to his advisors.

sens: Interjection serving to attract attention
Marker of a comparison or resemblance
H1888B.detail:
1. This Hebrew interjection calls the listener to look, to pay attention to what follows: "Here" or "Look." It creates a pause and marks a turning point in the discourse, like when one says "Listen well" before announcing something important.
2. In Aramaic (the language spoken in Babylon), it introduces a comparison or states a similarity: "just as," "just like." In Daniel 2:43, the expression "here you have seen" introduces the interpretation of a vision and the enumeration of resemblances: the feet of the statue are partly iron and partly clay, "here" that the descendants of kings will mingle by marriage, but without forming a solid block — just as iron does not unite with clay.
H1888B.origine: This word comes from the Hebrew verb הִרְאָה (hir'a), meaning "to see" or "to show." The interjection הֵא in biblical Hebrew and its Aramaic equivalent retain this root: one shows something to someone by saying "Here!" It is a very ancient word, common in both Semitic languages. In Aramaic particularly, it serves as a logical and temporal hinge.
H1888B.emploi: This interjection appears once in the preserved Hebrew Bible (Daniel 2:43, in Aramaic). It is typical of prophetic speeches and explanations: the prophet or interpreter uses it to punctuate the narrative and guide the listener step by step. In the biblical Aramaic context (notably Daniel and Ezra), it often marks a transition between the exposition of a riddle and its resolution.
